steps.overview: This step gets Claude Code installed, signed in and running in a real project. You will learn how Claude Code explores a repository, uses tools to read files and run commands, and asks your permission before it acts. These basics (sessions, permission prompts and undo) come up in every later step and in the Claude Code in Action course.
objectives: Install Claude Code with the native installer or npm, then sign in with a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console account
Start an interactive session with `claude` in a project folder and ask it to explain the codebase and list its entry points
Approve, deny or always-allow a tool call, and switch permission modes with Shift+Tab
Undo Claude's file edits with checkpoints (Esc Esc or /rewind) and with git
Choose the right surface for a task: terminal, VS Code extension, JetBrains plugin, desktop app or Claude Code on the web

concepts.explanation: The recommended install is the native installer: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` on macOS, Linux or WSL, or `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` in Windows PowerShell. The native build updates itself in the background. The npm route is `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` and needs Node.js 18 or newer. Never use sudo with npm global installs. Run `claude doctor` to check the installation.

On first run, Claude Code opens a browser login. You can sign in with a Claude subscription (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise) or with an Anthropic Console account, which bills by API usage. Enterprise users can also go through Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI or Microsoft Foundry. Inside a session, use /login to switch accounts and /logout to sign out.

Run `claude` from the project root to start a REPL scoped to that folder. Claude Code does not index the whole repo upfront. It explores step by step with search and read tools, the way an engineer would. Use `claude -c` to continue the most recent conversation, `claude -r` to pick an older one, and `claude -p "query"` for a one-shot, non-interactive answer.

Claude acts only through tools. Read, Glob and Grep read and search files. Edit and Write change files. Bash runs shell commands. WebFetch and WebSearch reach the web. Each tool call appears in the transcript, so you can see exactly what Claude read, ran or changed.

Read-only actions such as reading and searching files run without asking. File edits and most Bash commands need approval. A prompt offers three choices: Yes; Yes and don't ask again (for that command or for edits this session); or No, where you tell Claude what to do differently. Denying is safe, because Claude simply changes its plan.

Press Shift+Tab to cycle the modes. Default mode asks before edits and commands. Accept-edits mode auto-approves file edits. Plan mode is read-only: Claude researches and proposes a plan but changes nothing. Bypass mode (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`) skips all prompts and is meant only for isolated sandboxes or containers.

Claude Code saves a checkpoint before each edit it makes. Press Esc twice, or run /rewind, to restore the code, the conversation, or both, to an earlier point. Checkpoints only track Claude's own file edits. They do not undo Bash side effects such as deleted files, migrations or git pushes, so keep git as your real safety net.

/init scans the repo and writes a CLAUDE.md file. It records build and test commands, architecture notes and conventions. Claude Code loads this file into context at the start of every session in that project. Commit it so the whole team shares the same project memory.

The VS Code extension (also works in Cursor and Windsurf) gives a graphical panel with inline diffs. The JetBrains plugin covers IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm and others; it runs Claude Code from the IDE terminal and shows diffs in the IDE viewer. The desktop app and Claude Code on the web (claude.ai/code) run sessions without a local terminal. Web sessions run in cloud sandboxes against your GitHub repositories.

keyFacts: npm install needs Node.js 18+, and the package name is @anthropic-ai/claude-code. The native installer is the recommended option and auto-updates.
`claude` starts an interactive session. `claude -p` is one-shot print mode. `-c` continues the last session. `-r` resumes a chosen session.
Reading and searching files needs no approval. Edits and Bash commands ask first, unless an allow rule or a permission mode covers them.
Shift+Tab cycles the modes: default, then auto-accept edits, then plan mode. Plan mode never modifies files.
Press Esc once to interrupt Claude mid-task. Press Esc twice, or run /rewind, to restore a checkpoint.
Checkpoints do not revert Bash side effects or changes made outside Claude Code. Use git for those.
Use @path/to/file to pull a file into context. Start a line with ! to run a shell command directly.
Useful commands: /help, /init, /clear (fresh context), /compact (summarise context), /permissions, /model, /status, /ide (connect an external terminal to your IDE).
Permission rules live in .claude/settings.json under allow, ask and deny, for example "Bash(npm run test:*)". Deny rules take precedence over allow rules.

example.caption: Install, start a session and explore an unfamiliar repo safely
example.code:
# 1. Install (macOS/Linux/WSL) - or: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
claude doctor            # verify install

# 2. Clone an unfamiliar repo and start a session
git clone https://github.com/expressjs/express.git && cd express
git status               # clean tree = easy undo later
claude                   # browser login on first run

# 3. Inside the session (press Shift+Tab until 'plan mode' for read-only):
# > Explain this codebase: purpose, folder layout, and main modules.
# > List every entry point (package.json main/bin/exports, scripts,
#   CLI files, server start files) as a table with file paths.
# > /init                 # writes CLAUDE.md; approve the Write prompt

# 4. Practise a deny and an undo:
# > Add a comment at the top of index.js explaining the export
#   -> choose 'No' and say: 'put it in lib/express.js instead'
#   -> approve the new edit, then press Esc Esc and rewind the code

# 5. Confirm nothing unexpected changed
git status && git diff

pitfalls: Running `claude` from your home folder instead of the project root. Claude's working scope and CLAUDE.md loading follow the launch directory.
Assuming /rewind undoes everything. It restores Claude's file edits only, not `rm`, database migrations, installs or pushes made through Bash.
Clicking 'Yes, and don't ask again' on broad Bash commands early on. Prefer narrow allow rules such as Bash(npm run test:*).
Using --dangerously-skip-permissions on your own machine. It is meant for isolated containers or sandboxes only.
Installing via npm with sudo, or on Node.js older than 18. This causes permission and runtime errors. Use the native installer instead.
Expecting Claude to know the whole repo instantly. It explores with tools, so ask it to search and read first, or use plan mode for big questions.

objective.question: A developer wants to install Claude Code with npm on a machine that runs Node.js 16. What should they do first?
options: Run npm install -g claude-code; the package works on any Node.js version
Nothing. Node.js 16 is supported if they add the --legacy flag
Install Python 3, because the npm package wraps a Python CLI
Upgrade to Node.js 18 or later, then run npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
objective.explanation: The npm install needs Node.js 18 or later, and the package name is @anthropic-ai/claude-code. The name 'claude-code' is wrong, Python is not needed, and no flag makes Node.js 16 supported.

objective.question: Your team lead asks which installation method Anthropic recommends for Claude Code and why. What is the best answer?
options: Building from source, because it gives the newest features
The native installer, because it is the recommended option and updates itself automatically
A Docker image, because Claude Code cannot run directly on a laptop
npm, because it is the only method that supports sign-in
objective.explanation: The native installer is the recommended method, and it auto-updates. npm also supports sign-in, and building from source or Docker are not the standard recommended paths.

objective.question: You want a shell script to send Claude Code one question, print the answer to stdout and exit, with no interactive session. Which invocation fits?
options: claude -p "summarise the changes"
claude /init "summarise the changes"
claude -r "summarise the changes"
claude -c "summarise the changes"
objective.explanation: -p is one-shot print mode: it answers and exits, so it suits scripts. -c continues the last session, -r resumes a session you choose, and /init is a slash command used inside a session.

objective.question: Yesterday you had several Claude Code sessions in the same project. Today you want to reopen the second-to-last one, not the most recent. Which flag do you use?
options: -p, because print mode restores history
-r, because it lets you pick which session to resume
--init, because it reloads CLAUDE.md and history
-c, because it lists every past session
objective.explanation: -r resumes a session you choose from a list. -c only continues the most recent session, -p is one-shot print mode, and --init is not a resume flag.

objective.question: In default permission mode, you ask Claude Code to find every file that imports a logger and then fix one of them. Which step triggers a permission prompt?
options: Reading the matching files
Editing the file to apply the fix
Listing the directory structure
Searching the codebase for import statements
objective.explanation: Reading and searching files need no approval. Editing files and running Bash commands ask first, unless an allow rule or a permission mode covers them.

objective.question: You have just cloned an unfamiliar repository. You want Claude Code to study it and propose a refactor, with a guarantee that no files change while you review the plan. Which mode do you use?
options: Default mode with all prompts approved
Print mode with -p
Auto-accept edits mode
Plan mode
objective.explanation: Plan mode researches and proposes, and it never modifies files. Auto-accept edits would apply changes, default mode still allows edits once you approve them, and -p is an output style, not a safety mode.

objective.question: You are in default mode and press Shift+Tab twice. Which mode are you in now?
options: Plan mode
Default mode again
Bypass permissions mode
Auto-accept edits mode
objective.explanation: Shift+Tab cycles default, then auto-accept edits, then plan mode. Two presses from default land on plan mode.

objective.question: Claude Code edited three source files. It also ran a Bash command that deleted a generated folder and applied a migration to your local database. You run /rewind to the checkpoint taken before these actions. What happens?
options: Only the database is restored, because migrations are tracked
The three file edits are reverted, but the deleted folder and the database changes are not
Nothing is restored, because Bash was used in the same turn
Everything is restored, including the folder and the database
objective.explanation: Checkpoints track file edits made by Claude's editing tools. They do not revert Bash side effects or changes made outside Claude Code, so use git and backups for those.

objective.question: The allow list in .claude/settings.json contains "Bash(git:*)" and the deny list contains "Bash(git push:*)". Claude tries to run git push origin main. What happens?
options: It prompts, because conflicting rules always fall back to ask
It runs only if the session is in auto-accept edits mode
It is blocked, because deny rules take precedence over allow rules
It runs without a prompt, because allow is checked first
objective.explanation: Deny rules take precedence over allow rules, so a matching deny blocks the command. Auto-accept edits mode covers file edits, not denied Bash commands.

objective.question: You want Claude Code to run any of your npm test scripts, such as npm run test:unit and npm run test:e2e, without prompting. Which rule belongs in the allow list?
options: "Edit(npm run test)"
"npm run test"
"Read(npm run test:*)"
"Bash(npm run test:*)"
objective.explanation: Bash permission rules use the Tool(pattern) form, and the :* suffix matches commands that start with the given prefix. Edit and Read are file tools, and a bare string has no tool name.

objective.question: After a long debugging session, responses feel slow and the context is full. You still need the key findings, but you can drop the detail. Which command fits best?
options: /init
/compact
/status
/clear
objective.explanation: /compact summarises the conversation, so key information stays and space is freed. /clear starts with a fresh, empty context, /init creates CLAUDE.md, and /status shows session information.

objective.question: Inside a Claude Code session, you want to run git status yourself and have its output appear in the conversation, without asking Claude to run it. What do you type?
options: /git status
!git status
#git status
@git status
objective.explanation: A line that starts with ! runs a shell command directly. @ references files, / starts slash commands, and # is not the shell-command prefix.

objective.question: You want Claude to look at src/server/app.ts while it answers your next question. What is the most direct way to do this?
options: Include @src/server/app.ts in your prompt
Run !cat src/server/app.ts and then /compact
Add the path to the deny list
Type /open src/server/app.ts
objective.explanation: @path/to/file pulls that file into context. /open is not the method taught for this, the ! route works but is indirect, and the deny list blocks access.

objective.question: You run Claude Code in a separate terminal app, not in the VS Code integrated terminal. You want it to see your open files, selections and diagnostics in VS Code. What do you do?
options: Reinstall Claude Code with npm instead of the native installer
Start a new session with claude -p
Add "IDE(*)" to the allow list
Run /ide in the session to connect it to the IDE
objective.explanation: /ide connects a Claude Code session in an external terminal to your IDE. The install method and print mode do not connect the IDE, and "IDE(*)" is not a valid permission rule.

subjective.question: Compare installing Claude Code with the native installer and with npm. Which would you recommend for a new team member, and why?
subjective.answer: There are two main ways to install Claude Code. The native installer is Anthropic's recommended option. It installs a standalone binary and updates itself automatically, so the developer stays on a current version without extra steps. The npm route is npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code. It needs Node.js 18 or later on the machine. npm can still make sense where Node.js is already standard and teams manage global packages through npm. For a new team member, I would recommend the native installer. It has fewer moving parts, has no Node.js version dependency, and keeps itself updated. After installing, they run claude in a project folder and sign in. Then a quick check such as /status confirms the version, the account and the model, so we know the setup works.
keyPoints: Native installer is recommended and auto-updates
npm package is @anthropic-ai/claude-code and needs Node.js 18+
npm suits teams already standardised on Node tooling
Verify the setup after sign-in, for example with /status

subjective.question: How do you authenticate Claude Code, and what should a developer check if it bills the wrong account?
subjective.answer: The first time you run claude, it asks you to sign in. There are two common ways. You can log in with a Claude subscription account, such as Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise. Or you can use an Anthropic Console account, which is billed by API usage. Enterprises can also route Claude Code through cloud providers such as Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex AI by setting the correct environment variables. If usage goes to the wrong account, run /status first. It shows which account and method are active. Then check whether an API key environment variable is set, because it can take priority over the subscription login. Use /logout and then /login to switch accounts. On a shared machine, never commit API keys to the repository. Keep credentials per user.
keyPoints: Sign-in happens on first run; /login and /logout switch accounts
Options: Claude subscription or Anthropic Console API billing
Bedrock and Vertex AI are possible for enterprises
/status shows the active auth; an API key env var can override the login

subjective.question: Walk through how you would use Claude Code to understand an unfamiliar repository and list its entry points.
subjective.answer: First, I cd into the repository root and run claude, so the session is scoped to that project. I would switch to plan mode with Shift+Tab, because I only want analysis and no edits. Then I ask something like: explain this codebase's architecture, list its entry points such as main files, CLI commands, server start-up, scheduled jobs and exported library APIs, and say how each one is triggered. Claude reads and searches files without approval. It will look at package manifests, build configs and source folders. Next, I verify its answers. I open the files it names with @path references, or run commands myself with !. Finally, I run /init. This creates a CLAUDE.md that records the structure and the build and test commands, so future sessions start with this context already loaded.
keyPoints: Start claude at the repo root; use plan mode for read-only analysis
Ask for entry points: main files, CLI, server start-up, jobs, exports
Reading and searching need no approval
Verify the claims with @file references and ! commands
Use /init to save the findings in CLAUDE.md

subjective.question: Explain how Claude Code's tools and permission prompts work during a normal session.
subjective.answer: Claude Code works through tools. It reads files, searches with glob and grep, edits or writes files, runs Bash commands, and can fetch web content. Read-only actions, such as reading and searching files, run without approval. Actions that change things ask first. These are file edits and Bash commands. When Claude wants to run one, the prompt shows the exact command or a diff of the edit. I can approve it once, approve it and tell Claude not to ask again for similar actions, or deny it and add a correction. If I deny, Claude does not run the action and usually suggests another approach. Allow rules in settings, or a mode such as auto-accept edits, can skip some prompts. This design keeps me in control of every side effect, which matters most in an unfamiliar repository.
keyPoints: Tools: read, search, edit/write, Bash, web fetch
Read and search run without approval; edits and Bash ask first
A prompt shows the command or diff; you can approve once, always or deny
Allow rules and permission modes can skip prompts

subjective.question: Describe the permission modes you can cycle with Shift+Tab, and give a situation for each.
subjective.answer: Shift+Tab cycles three modes in order: default, auto-accept edits and plan mode. Default mode asks before every file edit and Bash command that an allow rule does not cover. I use it in unfamiliar code, or for any risky task. Auto-accept edits applies file changes without prompting, but Bash commands still ask. It suits a well-understood task, such as renaming across many files, where I will review the diff in git afterwards. Plan mode lets Claude read and research, and then propose a plan. It never modifies files. I use it before large changes, or when I first explore a new codebase, and then I approve the plan and switch mode to carry it out. There is also a bypass permissions mode for isolated environments such as containers. I would not use it on a normal laptop.
keyPoints: Order: default, then auto-accept edits, then plan
Default prompts for edits and Bash
Auto-accept edits skips edit prompts only; Bash still asks
Plan mode never modifies files
Bypass mode is only for isolated sandboxes

subjective.question: What are checkpoints in Claude Code, how do you restore one, and what are their limits?
subjective.answer: Claude Code creates a checkpoint at each prompt, before it changes files, so you can go back if a direction turns out badly. To restore, press Esc twice or run /rewind. Then choose the point to return to. You can usually restore the code, the conversation or both, so you can keep the discussion but undo the edits. The limit is important. Checkpoints only track edits made through Claude's file editing tools. They do not undo Bash side effects, such as deleted folders, installed packages, database migrations or network calls. They also do not undo changes made outside Claude Code, for example by me in my editor. So checkpoints are a quick local undo, not version control. I still commit to git before larger tasks and keep backups for databases.
keyPoints: A checkpoint is taken before Claude's edits at each prompt
Restore with Esc Esc or /rewind; choose code, conversation or both
They do not revert Bash side effects
They do not revert changes made outside Claude Code
Use git commits as the real safety net

subjective.question: What is CLAUDE.md, what does /init do, and what would you put in the file?
subjective.answer: CLAUDE.md is a memory file that Claude Code loads into context automatically at the start of a session. It gives persistent project instructions, so I do not have to repeat them. /init analyses the codebase and creates a starting CLAUDE.md with its findings. I then edit the file by hand. Good content is short and practical. It covers build, test and lint commands, the project layout, coding conventions, branch and commit rules, and warnings such as 'do not edit generated files in /dist'. The project CLAUDE.md is committed to git, so the whole team shares it. A user-level file in ~/.claude holds my personal preferences. I keep it brief, because everything in it uses context on every session. I update it whenever Claude makes a repeated mistake.
keyPoints: Loaded automatically at session start as persistent instructions
/init generates a first draft from the codebase
Include commands, structure, conventions and warnings
Commit the project file; personal preferences go in the user-level file
Keep it concise because it uses context

subjective.question: Design permission rules for a team repository. Where do they live, and how do allow, ask and deny interact?
subjective.answer: Shared rules go in .claude/settings.json, which is committed so the whole team gets them. Personal overrides go in .claude/settings.local.json, which is not committed, and user-wide settings live in ~/.claude/settings.json. Under permissions, there are three lists: allow, ask and deny. For example, I would allow "Bash(npm run test:*)" and "Bash(npm run lint)", so routine checks run without prompts. I would put "Bash(git push:*)" in ask, so a person always confirms a push. I would deny reading secrets, for example "Read(./.env)", and deny dangerous commands. Deny rules take precedence over allow rules. So a broad allow, such as "Bash(git:*)", cannot override a specific deny. I can check the active rules with /permissions. The principle is least privilege: allow only safe, frequent actions.
keyPoints: .claude/settings.json is shared; settings.local.json is personal; ~/.claude is user-wide
Three lists: allow, ask and deny
Rule syntax such as "Bash(npm run test:*)"
Deny takes precedence over allow
Review the rules with /permissions; apply least privilege

subjective.question: Claude Code is halfway through a task and going in the wrong direction. What do you do, and how does pressing Esc once differ from pressing it twice?
subjective.answer: Pressing Esc once interrupts Claude straight away, but it keeps the session and the work done so far. I then type a correction, such as 'stop, use the existing helper in utils/date.ts instead', and Claude continues with that guidance. This is the best choice when the general direction is fine but needs steering. Pressing Esc twice opens the rewind menu, which is the same as running /rewind. There I pick an earlier checkpoint and restore the code, the conversation or both. I use this when the edits are wrong and I want a clean restart from a known point. If Claude already ran Bash commands with side effects, rewinding will not undo them. So I also check git status and revert manually if needed.
keyPoints: Esc once interrupts and keeps the context, so you can redirect
Esc twice equals /rewind, which restores a checkpoint
Choose to restore the code, the conversation or both
Check git status for Bash side effects that rewind cannot undo

subjective.question: How do you manage context in a long Claude Code session? Compare /clear and /compact.
subjective.answer: Everything in a session uses the context window: my prompts, the files Claude read, command output and its replies. When the context gets full, quality and speed can drop. /compact summarises the conversation so far and replaces the detail with a shorter summary. I use it when I am still on the same task and need the key decisions kept. I can give it instructions about what to keep. /clear wipes the conversation and starts with a fresh context in the same project. I use it when I switch to an unrelated task, so old details do not confuse Claude. CLAUDE.md is still loaded after either command, so project rules stay. Good habits: one task per session, reference specific files with @ rather than asking Claude to read everything, and check usage with /status or /context.
keyPoints: Prompts, files read and output all use context
/compact summarises and keeps key information
/clear starts fresh; use it for unrelated tasks
CLAUDE.md is reloaded either way
Use targeted @file references and keep one task per session

subjective.question: Claude Code runs in the terminal, VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, a desktop app and the web. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: The terminal CLI is the core experience and the most flexible option. It also supports scripting with -p. The VS Code extension, which also works in forks such as Cursor, gives a native panel. It shows proposed edits as inline diffs and shares the open file and selection with Claude. I prefer it when I want to review changes visually. The JetBrains plugin, for IntelliJ, PyCharm and similar IDEs, runs Claude Code and connects to the IDE's diff viewer and diagnostics. If I run claude in a separate terminal, /ide links it to the IDE. The desktop app suits people who want a dedicated window without an IDE. Claude Code on the web runs tasks in cloud environments against a GitHub repository. This is useful for parallel or long tasks, or when I am away from my machine.
keyPoints: CLI: core, flexible, scriptable
VS Code: inline diffs, shares open file and selection
JetBrains: IDE diff viewer and diagnostics; /ide connects external terminals
Desktop app: dedicated window without an IDE
Web: cloud runs on GitHub repos for parallel or remote work

subjective.question: How would you use claude -p safely in a script, and how is it different from an interactive session?
subjective.answer: claude -p "prompt" runs one request in print mode. It prints the result to stdout and exits. That makes it easy to use in shell pipelines, for example cat error.log | claude -p "explain the root cause". An interactive session keeps a conversation going and shows permission prompts. In a script, nobody is there to answer a prompt. So I define exactly which tools are allowed, using allow rules in settings or the allowed tools flag, and keep that list narrow. Read-only analysis tasks are the safest. For anything that edits code, I run it on a branch or in a container and review the diff before merging. I never give broad Bash access in unattended runs, especially on untrusted input. Output can also be requested in JSON when another program needs to parse it.
keyPoints: -p is one-shot: answer to stdout, then exit
Good for pipes and scripts; no interactive prompts
Pre-approve a narrow set of tools
Prefer read-only tasks; isolate any runs that edit code
JSON output is available for parsing

subjective.question: You deny a tool call that Claude proposed. What happens next, and how do you make the denial more useful?
subjective.answer: When I deny, Claude does not run that command or apply that edit, and the turn goes back to me. A bare denial tells Claude only 'no'. So it is better to deny and explain why, and give the alternative. For example: 'no, do not run npm install; the dependencies are already installed, just run the tests'. Or: 'do not edit the generated client; change the OpenAPI spec instead'. Claude then adjusts its plan. If I would always deny that kind of action, I add a deny rule in .claude/settings.json or through /permissions. Then it is blocked automatically in future sessions. If I find myself approving the same safe command again and again, I add an allow rule instead. Both reduce prompt fatigue without losing control.
keyPoints: A denied action is not executed
Add a reason and an alternative so Claude can adapt
Turn repeated denials into deny rules
Turn repeated safe approvals into allow rules
Manage rules with /permissions or settings.json

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: why not just turn on bypass permissions to save time when exploring a cloned open-source repository? How do you answer?
subjective.answer: I would say no, for safety reasons. An unfamiliar repository is untrusted input. Its files, READMEs or scripts can contain instructions that try to make the agent run harmful commands. This is prompt injection. With permissions bypassed, Claude could run Bash commands, install packages or send data without me seeing them first. Checkpoints would not save me, because they do not revert Bash side effects. The safer workflow is plan mode for exploration, because it never modifies files. Reading and searching need no approval anyway, so exploration is still fast. When I do need to run commands, I approve them one by one or allow a narrow set, such as test scripts. Bypass mode is only acceptable in an isolated container or VM with no secrets and limited network access.
keyPoints: Unfamiliar repos are untrusted; prompt injection is a risk
Bypass removes review of Bash and edits
Checkpoints cannot undo Bash side effects
Plan mode plus free read access is fast and safe
Bypass only in isolated sandboxes

steps.overview: This step teaches you how to give Claude Code lasting project memory with CLAUDE.md files. CLAUDE.md is loaded into context at the start of every session, so Claude knows your test command, lint command, conventions and no-go areas without being told again. The Claude Code in Action course treats memory as a core skill, and it is the cheapest way to make Claude reliable on a real codebase.
objectives: Generate a starter CLAUDE.md with /init and refine it by hand
Choose the right memory location: project, user, local or managed policy
Write precise test, lint and build commands plus do-not-touch rules that Claude follows
Use @imports and /memory to organise and edit memory without bloating it
Verify in a fresh session that Claude picks up the memory on its own

concepts.explanation: A Markdown file that Claude Code reads automatically at session start and adds to its context. It holds instructions you would otherwise repeat every time: commands, conventions, architecture notes. It is plain text guidance, not enforced configuration, so Claude follows it the way it follows any prompt.

A slash command that makes Claude scan the repository (package files, scripts, structure, existing docs) and write a starter CLAUDE.md. Treat the output as a draft: check every command it lists, delete generic advice and add what only your team knows.

./CLAUDE.md (or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md) at the repo root, committed to git and shared with the team. Put team-wide facts here: how to test, lint and build, code style, architecture and protected files. Every teammate's Claude gets the same instructions.

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md in your home directory, applied to every project on your machine. Use it for personal preferences, for example 'explain changes briefly' or your preferred commit message style. Do not put project-specific commands here.

CLAUDE.local.md at the project root, for your personal notes on this one repo, such as your local DB URL or sandbox account. Keep it out of version control by adding it to .gitignore. An alternative is to @import a file from your home directory so it works across git worktrees.

A CLAUDE.md placed at a system-level path by IT, for example /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md on Linux. It applies to all users on the machine and carries organisation-wide rules such as security policies. Individual developers normally do not edit it.

Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md files from the current working directory upward toward the root, so a monorepo can have a root file plus package-level files. CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories below the working directory are loaded on demand when Claude works with files in those folders. More specific files add detail on top of broader ones.

Inside CLAUDE.md you can write @path/to/file, for example @docs/testing.md, to pull another file into memory. Relative and home paths (@~/.claude/my-notes.md) both work, and imports can be nested up to a limited depth. Use imports to link existing docs instead of copying them.

Opens the loaded memory files in your editor and shows which files are active in the current session. Use it to check what Claude actually sees and to make quick edits. You can also just ask Claude to add a rule to CLAUDE.md.

Project memory: ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, committed to git, shared with the team.
User memory: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, applies to all your projects.
Local memory: CLAUDE.local.md, personal to one repo; keep it gitignored.
Managed policy memory sits at a system path and applies organisation-wide.
Memory is loaded at session start and uses context tokens in every session, so shorter memory is cheaper and gets followed better.
Specific beats vague: 'Run npm run test:unit -- path/to/file for one file' beats 'test your code'.
Import other files with @path syntax instead of pasting long docs into CLAUDE.md.

example.caption: A short project CLAUDE.md for a Node/TypeScript repo (Markdown content)
example.code:
# Project: orders-api (Node 20, TypeScript, Express)

## Commands
- Install: npm ci
- Test all: npm test
- Test one file: npx vitest run src/orders/orders.test.ts
- Lint: npm run lint   (fix: npm run lint -- --fix)
- Type check: npx tsc --noEmit
- Before saying a task is done: run lint, type check and tests.

## Code style
- 2-space indent, single quotes, no default exports.
- Use zod for request validation; schemas live in src/schemas/.
- New endpoints need a test in the same folder (*.test.ts).

## Architecture
- src/routes -> src/services -> src/db. Routes never call db directly.

## Do not touch
- src/db/migrations/ (already applied; create a new migration instead)
- .env and any file under secrets/
- package-lock.json unless adding a dependency

## More detail
- Testing guide: @docs/testing.md

pitfalls: Accepting /init output blindly. It can list scripts that are broken or miss the real test command; run each command once to confirm it works.
Writing vague rules like 'write clean code'. Claude cannot act on them, and they waste context in every session.
Letting CLAUDE.md grow into a long wiki. Long memory costs tokens every session and important rules get diluted; move detail into @imported docs.
Putting personal settings or secrets in the committed ./CLAUDE.md. Use CLAUDE.local.md or user memory, and never store credentials in memory.
Expecting CLAUDE.md to block actions. It is advice; hard rules need permission settings or hooks.
Testing the checkpoint in the same session. Memory is read at session start, so start a new session to prove Claude picks it up unprompted.

subjective.question: What does /init do in Claude Code, and what should you do after running it?
subjective.answer: /init scans the codebase and generates a starter CLAUDE.md. It usually picks up things like the language, framework, folder layout and commands it can find in files such as package.json or a Makefile. It is a good first draft, not a finished file. After running it, I read every line. I delete anything generic or obvious, like 'write clean code'. I correct commands that are wrong or incomplete, for example adding how to run a single test file. I add the things a scan cannot know: team conventions, do-not-touch folders and gotchas. Then I commit it so the team shares it. Finally, I open a new session and check that Claude follows it.

Output is a draft; always review
Trim generic or obvious content

Commit and verify in a new session

subjective.question: Explain the difference between project, user and local memory in Claude Code, with one example of what goes in each.
subjective.answer: Project memory lives at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md. It is committed to git and shared with the team. Example: 'Run npm run lint and npm run test:unit before finishing a task.' User memory lives at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. It applies to all my projects on my machine and is not shared. Example: 'Keep explanations short and show diffs, not full files.' Local memory is CLAUDE.local.md in one repo. It is personal to that repo and should be gitignored. Example: 'My local Postgres runs on port 5433 via docker compose.' The rule of thumb: shared team facts go in project memory, personal habits across projects go in user memory, and personal details for one repo go in local memory.

User: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, all your projects, personal
Local: CLAUDE.local.md, one repo, gitignored
Choose scope by who needs it and where

subjective.question: What is managed (enterprise) policy memory and when would an organisation use it?
subjective.answer: Managed policy memory is a CLAUDE.md placed at a system-level path, usually deployed by IT or platform teams. It applies to every Claude Code user on those machines, across all repos. An organisation would use it for instructions that must be consistent company-wide, such as 'never paste customer data into prompts', 'follow our secure coding standard', or 'use the internal package registry'. It saves each team from copying the same text into every repo. However, it is still guidance to the model, like any CLAUDE.md. If a rule must never be broken, for example blocking certain commands or file paths, the organisation should also use managed settings, permissions or hooks to enforce it.
keyPoints: CLAUDE.md at a system path
Applies organisation-wide to all users and repos
Used for consistent company policies
Deployed centrally, not per repo
Still guidance; enforce hard rules with permissions or hooks

subjective.question: Why should CLAUDE.md be kept short? Give practical ways to keep it short.
subjective.answer: CLAUDE.md is loaded at the start of every session and uses context tokens every time. A long file costs more tokens, leaves less room for the actual work, and important rules get buried, so Claude follows them less reliably. To keep it short, I include only what Claude needs in most sessions: commands, key conventions and do-not-touch areas. I write each rule as one specific line. I remove anything Claude can learn by reading the code, like listing every folder. I move long material, such as an API style guide or architecture notes, into separate files and reference them with @imports. I put package-specific rules in nested CLAUDE.md files. I also review the file regularly and delete stale entries.
keyPoints: Loaded every session; costs context tokens
Short memory is followed better
One specific line per rule
Use @imports and nested files for detail
Prune stale content regularly

subjective.question: Hands-on: write a short CLAUDE.md section that tells Claude how to run tests and lint for a Node/TypeScript project. Explain your choices.
subjective.answer: Example section: '## Commands' then '- Install: npm ci' '- Lint: npm run lint (fix with npm run lint -- --fix)' '- Type check: npm run typecheck' '- Unit tests, one file: npm run test:unit -- path/to/file.test.ts' '- Unit tests, all: npm run test:unit' '- Before finishing any task: run lint, typecheck and the unit tests for changed files.' My choices: every line is an exact command Claude can copy, not advice like 'test your code'. I include the single-file form because it is faster, so Claude uses it during iteration. I add a clear 'before finishing' rule so Claude knows when to run them. I keep it to a few lines so it is cheap to load and easy to follow. Then I verify in a fresh session.
keyPoints: Exact, runnable commands
Single-file and full-suite variants
Clear trigger for when to run them
Short and scannable
Verify in a new session

subjective.question: How would you verify the checkpoint 'Claude runs the right test command in a new session without being told'?
subjective.answer: First I save and commit CLAUDE.md. Then I fully exit Claude Code and start a new session, so there is no chat history carrying the information. I can run /memory to confirm the project CLAUDE.md is in the loaded list. Next I give a normal task without mentioning tests, for example 'fix the off-by-one bug in utils/date.ts'. I watch the tool calls. Success means Claude runs the exact command from CLAUDE.md, ideally the single-file form for the changed test. If it guesses a different command, I make the line more specific or move it higher, then repeat in another fresh session. A test in the same session where I wrote the file proves nothing.
keyPoints: Use a genuinely fresh session
Confirm loading with /memory
Give a task without mentioning tests
Check the exact command Claude runs
Iterate on wording if it fails

subjective.question: What are @imports in CLAUDE.md and when should you use them instead of pasting content?
subjective.answer: @imports let CLAUDE.md pull in another file using @path syntax, for example '@docs/testing.md' or '@README.md'. The imported file becomes part of memory. I use imports when content is long, already exists elsewhere, or is maintained by another owner. Examples are an architecture document, an API style guide or a contributing guide. This keeps the main CLAUDE.md short and readable, avoids two copies drifting apart, and lets each document have one source of truth. I can also import a personal file from my home directory so personal notes stay out of the repo. The trade-off: imported content still uses context, so I import only files that are genuinely useful, not every document in the repo.
keyPoints: @path syntax pulls in another file
Keeps main CLAUDE.md short
Single source of truth; avoids drift
Can reference personal files outside the repo
Imported content still costs tokens

subjective.question: Explain how Claude Code finds and combines memory files, including nested CLAUDE.md files in a monorepo.
subjective.answer: At session start, Claude Code loads memory from several scopes: managed policy memory, user memory in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, and project memory. For project memory it looks in the current working directory and walks up through parent directories, loading CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files it finds. CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories below the working directory are not loaded up front; they are pulled in when Claude reads files in those subtrees. In a monorepo this is useful: the root CLAUDE.md holds shared commands and conventions, and packages/api/CLAUDE.md holds API-specific test commands. When Claude works in packages/api, both apply. More specific files add detail. I use /memory to check which files are actually loaded.
keyPoints: Multiple scopes: managed, user, project, local
Walks up from working directory to parents
Nested subfolder files load when Claude works there
Root for shared rules, nested for package rules
/memory confirms what is loaded

subjective.question: A teammate writes 'NEVER touch the payments folder' in CLAUDE.md and says the folder is now protected. How do you respond?
subjective.answer: I would say the line is useful but it is not protection. CLAUDE.md is guidance that shapes Claude's behaviour. It usually works, but it is not a guarantee. Claude could misread a task, lose the rule in a long context, or a user could ask for an edit directly. If the payments folder must never be changed by Claude, we need enforcement: permission rules that deny edits to that path, or a hook that blocks writes to it. We cover those in later steps. I would keep the CLAUDE.md line because it explains intent and avoids wasted attempts, and it also helps Claude suggest the right owner. So the answer is guidance plus enforcement, not guidance alone.
keyPoints: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforcement
Rules can be missed or overridden
Use permissions or hooks for hard rules
Keep the CLAUDE.md line to explain intent

subjective.question: What kinds of 'do-not-touch' rules belong in CLAUDE.md, and how should you write them?
subjective.answer: Do-not-touch rules cover areas Claude should not change without explicit approval. Examples: generated code like src/generated, database migration files already applied in production, vendored libraries, lock files, CI config, and secrets or .env files. I write each rule as one specific line with a path and a reason or alternative. For example: 'Do not edit src/generated/*; regenerate with npm run codegen.' or 'Do not modify applied migrations; create a new migration instead.' The reason helps Claude choose the right action instead of just stopping. I avoid vague lines like 'be careful with important files'. For anything critical, I also add a permission rule or hook, because CLAUDE.md alone does not block edits.
keyPoints: Generated code, applied migrations, vendored code, secrets, CI config
Name the exact path
Give the reason or correct alternative
Avoid vague wording
Back critical rules with permissions or hooks

subjective.question: Compare a vague and a specific CLAUDE.md instruction for coding conventions. Why does specificity matter?
subjective.answer: A vague instruction is 'Follow good style and write clean code.' Claude already tries to do that, so the line adds tokens but no new information. A specific version is: 'Use named exports, not default exports. Use zod for request validation. Put React components in src/components/<Name>/index.tsx with a co-located test file.' These lines describe choices that differ from project to project, so Claude cannot guess them. Specific rules are easier to follow and easier to check in review. They also reduce rework, because Claude gets it right the first time. My test for each line: would Claude probably do something different without it? If not, I delete it. Specific and project-unique beats general advice.
keyPoints: Vague lines add tokens but no information
Specific lines capture project-unique choices
Easier to follow and verify
Test: would Claude behave differently without it?

subjective.question: What does the /memory command do and when would you use it during real work?
subjective.answer: /memory shows the memory files loaded in the current session and lets me open one to edit it. I use it in three main situations. First, debugging: if Claude ignores a rule, I check whether the file containing that rule is actually loaded, for example whether I started in the wrong directory. Second, quick fixes: if I notice a wrong or outdated command, I open the right file through /memory and correct it straight away. Third, choosing scope: it reminds me which files exist, so I put a new rule in project, user or local memory as appropriate. After editing, I check the change in a new session, because memory is loaded at session start.
keyPoints: Lists memory files loaded in this session
Opens a file for editing
Debug ignored rules by checking what loaded
Fix commands quickly
Verify edits in a new session

subjective.question: Your team's CLAUDE.md is outdated: the test runner changed from Jest to Vitest but the file still says 'npm test uses Jest'. What risks does this create and how should teams maintain memory?
subjective.answer: Stale memory is worse than no memory. Claude trusts CLAUDE.md, so it may run old commands, write Jest-style mocks, or waste time debugging failures caused by the wrong tool. New teammates also get misled. To maintain it, treat CLAUDE.md like code. Update it in the same pull request that changes the tooling, so the reviewer checks both together. Keep commands in CLAUDE.md pointing to package scripts like 'npm run test:unit', so the script can change without the memory going stale. Review the file periodically and remove dead rules. When Claude repeatedly makes the same mistake, add or fix a line. Because the file is committed, git history shows who changed what and why.
keyPoints: Stale memory actively misleads Claude
Update CLAUDE.md in the same PR as tooling changes
Reference stable script names
Periodic review and pruning
Git history gives accountability

subjective.question: Design a memory setup for a developer who works on three repos for one company, has personal preferences, and has a company security policy to follow.
subjective.answer: I would use four layers. Managed policy memory, deployed by IT at the system path, holds company-wide rules such as secure coding and data handling. User memory in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md holds personal preferences that apply everywhere, like answer style or 'show a plan before large edits'. Each of the three repos has a committed project CLAUDE.md with its own build, test and lint commands, conventions and do-not-touch paths, plus @imports to longer docs. If a repo needs personal local details, such as custom ports, those go in a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md. I avoid repeating the same rule across layers, keep each file short, and confirm with /memory. Hard rules from the security policy are also enforced through permissions or hooks.
keyPoints: Managed policy for company-wide rules
User memory for personal cross-project preferences
Project memory per repo, committed
Local memory for personal repo details, gitignored
No duplication; enforce hard rules separately

steps.overview: This step teaches the core Claude Code working loop for anything bigger than a one-line fix. You explore and plan first, review the plan, then build against failing tests, with the right permissions and focused context. The Claude Code in Action course tests these habits directly. They also separate safe, reviewable AI-assisted changes from risky ones in real teams.
objectives: Use plan mode to get a reviewed, written plan from Claude before any file is edited.
Configure permission modes and allow, ask and deny rules in the correct settings.json file.
Supply precise context with @-mentions, pasted screenshots and linked GitHub issues.
Run a test-driven loop where Claude writes a failing test first, then makes it pass without changing the test.
Manage a long session with /compact, /clear and /context so Claude stays accurate.

concepts.explanation: Plan mode is a read-only permission mode. Claude can read files, search and reason, but it cannot edit files or run state-changing commands. It ends by presenting a plan that you approve, reject or refine. Toggle it with Shift+Tab, or start a session with `claude --permission-mode plan`.

This is Anthropic's recommended workflow for larger changes. First ask Claude to read the relevant files without writing code. Then ask for a plan and review it. Then let Claude implement and verify the change, and finally commit or open a PR. Skipping the explore and plan stages is the most common cause of wrong-direction edits.

`default` asks before edits and commands. `acceptEdits` auto-approves file edits for the session. `plan` is read-only. `bypassPermissions` skips all prompts and is meant only for isolated sandboxes or containers. Shift+Tab cycles through the everyday modes in the terminal. You can set a starting mode with `defaultMode` in settings.json.

The `permissions` object in settings.json holds three lists: `allow`, `ask` and `deny`. Rules look like `Bash(npm run test:*)`, `Read(./.env)`, `Edit` or `WebFetch(domain:github.com)`. Deny rules take precedence over allow rules. Use `/permissions` to view and edit rules interactively.

User settings live in `~/.claude/settings.json` and apply to all your projects. Shared project settings live in `.claude/settings.json` and are committed to git for the team. Personal project settings live in `.claude/settings.local.json`, which Claude Code configures git to ignore. Enterprise managed settings override everything else.

Type `@path/to/file` to pull a file into the prompt; `@` on a directory gives Claude its listing. Paste screenshots or mockups with Ctrl+V (on macOS too, not Cmd+V), or drag and drop an image. For issues, give the URL or number and let Claude read it with the `gh` CLI or a GitHub MCP server. CLAUDE.md holds context that should load automatically in every session.

Ask Claude to write tests for the expected behaviour, and say explicitly that you are doing TDD so it must not write the implementation. Have it run the tests and confirm they fail, then commit the tests. Next, ask it to write code that makes the tests pass without modifying the tests, iterating until they are green. Tests give Claude a clear, checkable target.

`/clear` wipes the conversation history; use it between unrelated tasks. `/compact` replaces history with a summary and can take focus instructions, e.g. `/compact keep the plan and failing test names`. Claude Code also auto-compacts when the context window nears its limit. `/context` shows what is using the context window.

Press Esc to stop Claude mid-action while keeping context, so you can redirect it. Press Esc twice to jump back in the history and edit an earlier prompt, or to rewind to a checkpoint. Course-correcting early is cheaper than undoing a large wrong diff.

keyFacts: Shift+Tab cycles permission modes in the terminal: default → auto-accept edits → plan mode.
Plan mode is read-only. Claude cannot edit files or run state-changing commands until you approve the plan.

subjective.question: What is plan mode in Claude Code, and when would you use it?
subjective.answer: Plan mode is a read-only permission mode. Claude can read files, search the codebase and think through the problem, but it cannot edit files or run state-changing commands until I approve its plan. I enter it with Shift+Tab, which cycles default, auto-accept edits and plan, or I start with `claude --permission-mode plan`. I use it for larger changes: a feature touching several files, a refactor, or work in a part of the codebase I do not know well. It separates thinking from doing. I see Claude's understanding of the problem before any code changes, so I can correct wrong assumptions cheaply. For a one-line fix or a typo, plan mode is overhead and I skip it.
keyPoints: Read-only: no edits or state-changing commands until approval
Entered via Shift+Tab cycle or `--permission-mode plan`
Best for multi-file features, refactors, unfamiliar code
Catches wrong assumptions before code is written
Skip it for trivial changes

subjective.question: Claude has produced a plan for your feature. How do you review it before approving edits?
subjective.answer: I read the plan as if it were a design review from a junior colleague. First, does it understand the goal correctly, including edge cases? Second, which files will it touch? If it plans to change files I did not expect, such as a shared utility or config, I ask why. Third, does it follow existing patterns in the codebase rather than inventing new ones? Fourth, does it include tests and say how it will verify the change? Fifth, is the scope right, with no extra 'improvements' I did not ask for? If anything is off, I stay in plan mode and give feedback, for example 'reuse the existing validator in utils/validate.ts'. I approve only when the plan is specific enough that I could predict the diff.
keyPoints: Check understanding of the goal and edge cases
Check which files will change and why
Check it follows existing codebase patterns
Check tests and a verification step are included
Iterate in plan mode before approving; watch for scope creep

subjective.question: Explain the 'explore, plan, code, commit' workflow and why each step matters.
subjective.answer: It is a four-step loop for non-trivial work. Explore: Claude reads the relevant files, often in plan mode or with an instruction not to write code yet. This builds the context it needs. Plan: Claude proposes a concrete approach, and I review and refine it. This is where mistakes are cheapest to fix. Code: after I approve, Claude implements the plan and checks its work by running tests or the linter. Commit: Claude writes a clear commit message and, if needed, opens a pull request, after I have reviewed the diff. The value is that Claude does not jump straight into coding. Without the explore and plan steps, it may solve the wrong problem or ignore existing patterns. The commit step keeps changes small and reversible.
keyPoints: Explore: read relevant code first, no edits
Plan: concrete approach reviewed by the developer
Code: implement and verify with tests
Commit: reviewed diff, clear message, small reversible change
Prevents jumping to code on the wrong problem

subjective.question: Compare the main permission modes in Claude Code: default, acceptEdits, plan and bypassPermissions.
subjective.answer: Default mode asks for permission the first time Claude wants to use each tool, such as editing a file or running a shell command, unless an allow rule already covers it. acceptEdits, or auto-accept edits, lets Claude edit files without asking, but it still asks before running commands not on the allow-list. I use it when I trust the plan and want speed. Plan mode is read-only: Claude researches and proposes a plan, and nothing changes until I approve. bypassPermissions, started with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, skips all prompts. It is only safe in an isolated container or VM with no sensitive access, because Claude can then run any command. In the terminal, Shift+Tab cycles default, auto-accept edits and plan.
keyPoints: Default: prompt on first use of each tool
acceptEdits: file edits auto-approved, commands still checked
Plan: read-only until plan approved
bypassPermissions: no prompts, isolated environments only
Shift+Tab cycles default → accept edits → plan

subjective.question: How do allow, ask and deny permission rules work, and what happens when they conflict?
subjective.answer: Permission rules live under `permissions` in settings.json. Allow rules let Claude use a tool without prompting, for example `Bash(npm run test:*)`. Ask rules force a confirmation prompt even if something else would allow it, which is useful for risky commands like `git push`. Deny rules block a tool entirely, for example `Read(./.env)` to protect secrets. When rules match the same action, deny wins over ask, and ask wins over allow. So if I allow broad reading of the project but deny `Read(./.env)`, the env file stays blocked. This lets me write generous allow-lists for speed and still keep a hard safety net. The `:*` suffix in Bash rules is a prefix match, so I write rules carefully to avoid allowing more than intended.
keyPoints: Allow: no prompt; ask: always confirm; deny: blocked
Conflict order: deny beats ask beats allow
Use deny for secrets like `Read(./.env)`
`Bash(cmd:*)` is a prefix match
Broad allows plus narrow denies give speed and safety

subjective.question: Describe the settings file scopes in Claude Code and their order of precedence. Which file would you commit?
subjective.answer: From highest to lowest precedence: enterprise managed settings, then command-line arguments, then `.claude/settings.local.json`, then `.claude/settings.json`, then the user file `~/.claude/settings.json`. Managed settings are set by an organisation and cannot be overridden, which suits security policy. CLI arguments apply to one launch. The local project file is for my personal rules in this repo and is git-ignored. The shared project file is committed to git, so the whole team gets the same allow and deny rules, such as allowing the test command and denying `.env` reads. The user file holds my personal defaults for every project. I commit `.claude/settings.json` only, and I keep personal experiments in the local file so I do not push my preferences onto the team.
keyPoints: Order: managed → CLI → local project → shared project → user
Managed settings cannot be overridden
Commit `.claude/settings.json` for team rules
`.claude/settings.local.json` is personal and git-ignored
`~/.claude/settings.json` holds personal defaults across projects

subjective.question: Write a project permissions block for a Node.js app so Claude can run tests and lint without prompts, must confirm before pushing, and can never read env files. Explain your choices.
subjective.answer: In `.claude/settings.json` I would write: `{"permissions": {"allow": ["Bash(npm run test:*)", "Bash(npm run lint)"], "ask": ["Bash(git push:*)"], "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)"]}}`. The test rule uses a prefix match, so `npm run test` and `npm run test:unit` run freely, which keeps a TDD loop fast. Lint is allowed as an exact command. Push is in ask because it affects the shared remote and should always get a human check. The deny rules cover `.env` and variants like `.env.local`. Because deny beats allow, these stay blocked even if someone later adds broad read access. I commit this file so the team shares it. I avoid rules like `Bash(npm:*)`, which would also allow `npm install` of arbitrary packages.
keyPoints: Allow test (prefix) and lint commands for fast loops
Put `git push` under ask
Deny `.env` and `.env.*` reads
Deny beats allow, so secrets stay protected
Avoid overly broad prefixes like `Bash(npm:*)`

subjective.question: What are the ways to give Claude Code good context for a task, and when would you use each?
subjective.answer: First, @ mentions. Typing `@src/cart.ts` pulls the file into context, and an @ on a directory gives a listing. I use this when I know exactly which files matter, so Claude does not waste time searching. Second, images. I paste screenshots with Ctrl+V, even on macOS, or drag them in. This is ideal for UI bugs, design mockups or error dialogs. Third, issues. I paste the issue text or URL, or ask Claude to read it with the `gh` CLI if it is installed. This gives requirements and acceptance criteria in the author's own words. I can also pipe in logs or paste error output. Good context is specific: point to the relevant code, show the symptom and state the expected outcome, and avoid dumping whole folders.
keyPoints: @ file pulls content; @ directory gives a listing
Ctrl+V pastes screenshots, including on macOS
Link or paste issues; `gh` CLI can fetch them
Paste logs and error output
Be specific; do not flood context

subjective.question: Walk through a test-driven loop with Claude Code for a new feature.
subjective.answer: Step one: I tell Claude we are doing TDD and ask it to write tests from the expected inputs and outputs, with no implementation yet. Step two: I ask it to run the tests and confirm they fail for the right reason, not because of a typo or import error. Step three: I review the tests, because they are the specification, and then commit them. Step four: I ask Claude to write code that makes the tests pass without changing the tests. It runs the suite, reads failures and iterates. An allow rule like `Bash(npm run test:*)` keeps this loop fast. Step five: when all tests pass, I review the diff and check that the implementation is general, not hard-coded to the test cases. Then I commit.
keyPoints: Write tests first, no implementation
Confirm tests fail for the right reason
Review and commit the tests as the spec
Implement without modifying tests; iterate on failures
Check for overfitting, then review diff and commit

subjective.question: Why should you tell Claude not to modify the tests during the implementation step, and what other risks do you watch for?
subjective.answer: The tests are the contract. If Claude is allowed to change them, the easiest route to green is to weaken an assertion, skip a case or delete a failing test. Then the suite passes but the feature is wrong. Committing the tests first makes any change to them visible in the diff. I also watch for overfitting, where the code special-cases the exact test inputs instead of solving the general problem. Asking Claude to explain its approach, or adding one extra test it has not seen, exposes this. Other risks are mocking too much, so the tests no longer exercise real behaviour, and tests that pass on the first run, which means they never failed and may test nothing. Line-by-line diff review catches most of these.
keyPoints: Tests are the specification; editing them hides failures
Commit tests first so changes show in the diff
Watch for code hard-coded to test inputs
Watch for over-mocking and tests that never failed
Review the diff line by line

subjective.question: Explain the difference between `/clear`, `/compact` and `/context`, with an example of when you would use each.
subjective.answer: `/clear` wipes the conversation history and starts fresh in the same session. I use it between unrelated tasks, for example after finishing a login feature and before fixing a CSV bug, so old details do not distract Claude. `/compact` summarises the conversation to free space but keeps the important thread. I can add focus instructions, like `/compact keep the API design decisions and the failing test names`. I use it in a long session that is still about the same task. `/context` shows how the context window is being used, including how much space files, tools and messages take. I use it to decide whether I need to compact, or to spot something large, like a big file or many MCP tools, eating context.
keyPoints: `/clear`: fresh start between unrelated tasks
`/compact [focus]`: summarise a long, relevant session
Focus instructions control what the summary keeps
`/context`: view what is using the context window
Long, noisy context lowers output quality

subjective.question: How do you interrupt and rewind Claude Code when it goes in the wrong direction?
subjective.answer: If Claude starts doing something wrong, I press Esc. That stops the current action but keeps the session and context, so I can redirect it straight away, for example 'stop, the bug is in the parser, not the router'. Pressing Esc twice lets me go back to an earlier message, edit it and continue from there. This is useful when my original prompt was the problem. Claude Code also keeps checkpoints of its file edits, and the `/rewind` command can restore code or conversation to an earlier point. Checkpoints do not undo external side effects such as database changes or a push, so git is still my main safety net. The habit is to correct early. A two-second interrupt is cheaper than reviewing a long wrong diff.
keyPoints: Esc interrupts while keeping the session
Double Esc goes back to edit an earlier message
Checkpoints and `/rewind` restore earlier states
Rewind does not undo external side effects; use git
Correct course early

subjective.question: A colleague says 'permission prompts slow me down, I just run with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.' How would you respond?
subjective.answer: I understand the frustration, but that flag turns on bypassPermissions, which means Claude can run any command with no checks. On a normal laptop that includes deleting files, pushing to remote, reading credentials, or acting on a prompt injection hidden in a web page or file. Reviewing the diff afterwards does not help, because commands have already run. If they really need it, for example for a long unattended migration, it should run only in an isolated container or VM with no sensitive access, no production credentials and limited network. For daily work, the better fix is a good allow-list: allow test, lint and build commands, use acceptEdits once the plan is approved, and keep deny rules for secrets. That removes most prompts while keeping safety.
keyPoints: The flag removes all permission checks
Risks: destructive commands, secret exposure, prompt injection
Only in isolated container or VM without sensitive access
Better: tuned allow-list plus acceptEdits
Keep deny rules for secrets

subjective.question: Describe how you would complete this week's task: use plan mode to add a feature with tests to a small app, and meet the checkpoint.
subjective.answer: I start a clean session with `/clear` and switch to plan mode. I describe the feature, @-mention the relevant files and paste any screenshot or issue text. Claude explores and proposes a plan. I check files, approach, tests and scope, and refine until I can predict the diff. After approval, I run a TDD loop: Claude writes failing tests, I confirm they fail for the right reason and commit them, then Claude implements without touching the tests. My project settings allow `npm run test:*` so the loop is fast, and deny `.env` reads. When tests pass, I run `git diff` and read every line: logic, edge cases, naming, no stray debug code, no unrelated changes. I ask Claude to explain anything unclear, run the full suite once more, then commit with a clear message.
keyPoints: Clean context, plan mode, @ mentions for relevant files
Review and refine the plan before approving
TDD: failing tests committed first, then implementation
Sensible allow and deny rules for a fast, safe loop
Line-by-line diff review and full test run before commit

steps.overview: This step teaches you to customise Claude Code for a team. You will use custom slash commands for repeatable prompts, skills for packaged know-how that Claude loads when relevant, and hooks for deterministic automation such as auto-formatting and blocking edits to protected files. You will also learn which settings files to commit so every teammate gets the same behaviour. These topics appear in the Claude Code in Action course and in real-world team setups.
objectives: Create a project slash command in .claude/commands that accepts arguments with $ARGUMENTS.
Write a skill in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md with a description that tells Claude when to load it.
Configure a PostToolUse hook that runs Prettier on every file Claude edits or writes.
Build a PreToolUse hook that uses exit code 2 to block edits to protected files.
Choose correctly between user, project and local settings files, and commit the right ones for the team.

concepts.explanation: A Markdown file whose body is a prompt template. Project commands live in .claude/commands/ and personal commands live in ~/.claude/commands/. The file name becomes the command, so review.md becomes /review. Subfolders help you organise commands, and /help lists the available ones.

$ARGUMENTS inserts everything typed after the command, and $1, $2 insert positional arguments. Optional YAML frontmatter can set description, argument-hint, allowed-tools and model. Inside a command, @path includes a file's contents and a line starting with ! runs a bash command whose output becomes context. A ! line needs a matching Bash entry in allowed-tools.

A skill is a folder containing SKILL.md, which has YAML frontmatter with name and description, plus optional scripts and reference files. At startup Claude reads only each skill's name and description. It loads the full content when the task matches that description; this is called progressive disclosure. Project skills live in .claude/skills/ and personal skills live in ~/.claude/skills/.

CLAUDE.md is always loaded, so use it for short, always-true project rules. A slash command runs when a human explicitly invokes it. A skill is loaded by Claude itself when relevant, so it suits longer, task-specific procedures that should not fill the context window all the time.

Hooks are shell commands that Claude Code runs automatically at lifecycle events. Unlike instructions in a prompt, they are deterministic: they always run. You configure them under the "hooks" key of a settings.json file, and you can view them with the /hooks command.

Key events are PreToolUse (before a tool runs, can block it), PostToolUse (after a tool succeeds), UserPromptSubmit, Notification, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, SessionStart and SessionEnd. For tool events, a matcher selects tools by name, for example "Edit|Write"; a regex is allowed. An empty matcher or "*" matches all tools.

The hook receives JSON on stdin with fields such as session_id, tool_name and tool_input; tool_input.file_path holds the edited file. Exit 0 means success. Exit 2 is a blocking error: in PreToolUse it cancels the tool call and sends stderr to Claude. Any other non-zero code is a non-blocking error that is shown to the user.

~/.claude/settings.json holds user settings for all projects. .claude/settings.json holds project settings; commit it to share hooks and permissions. .claude/settings.local.json holds personal overrides and is gitignored. Enterprise managed settings take the highest precedence.

keyFacts: review.md in .claude/commands/ is invoked as /review; ~/.claude/commands/ holds personal commands that work in every project.
$ARGUMENTS inserts the full argument string; $1, $2 insert positional arguments.
SKILL.md frontmatter requires name and description. The description decides when Claude loads the skill, so state both what the skill does and when to use it.
Exit code 2 from a PreToolUse hook blocks the tool call, and stderr is sent to Claude as feedback.
A PostToolUse hook cannot undo the action, because the tool has already run. Use it for formatting, linting and logging.
Use the matcher "Edit|Write" to catch file changes. Match MultiEdit too if your version exposes that tool.
$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR points to the project root, so reference hook scripts with it rather than relative paths.
Hooks have a default timeout of 60 seconds per command, which can be configured per hook.
Commit .claude/settings.json, .claude/commands/ and .claude/skills/. Keep .claude/settings.local.json out of git.
Hooks run with your user's full permissions. Review every hook command before adding it, especially hooks that come from others.

example.caption: .claude/settings.json (committed): blocks edits to .env and lockfiles, then runs Prettier after every edit. Requires jq and Prettier in the project.

pitfalls: Putting the team hook in .claude/settings.local.json or ~/.claude/settings.json. It works for you but teammates never get it, so the checkpoint fails.
Using exit code 1 to block an edit. Only exit code 2 blocks; other non-zero codes are just reported to the user as errors.
Trying to block in PostToolUse. By then the file is already changed, so protection belongs in PreToolUse.
Writing a vague skill description such as "helpers". Claude decides whether to load a skill from its description, so a vague one means the skill is never loaded.
Running Prettier on every file type. Without --ignore-unknown, edits to unsupported files produce errors on every change.
Hard-coding relative script paths in hooks. They break when Claude's working directory changes, so use $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.

workflow.title: Hands-on: Prettier hook plus shared /review command

steps.label: Install formatter and jq
steps.detail: Run npm install --save-dev prettier, and make sure jq is available on every developer machine.

steps.label: Add PostToolUse hook
steps.detail: In .claude/settings.json, add a PostToolUse entry with matcher "Edit|Write" that pipes tool_input.file_path into npx prettier --write.

steps.label: Add protected-file guard

subjective.question: Explain what a custom slash command is in Claude Code and how you create one for your team.
subjective.answer: A custom slash command is a saved prompt stored as a Markdown file. When I type the command, Claude Code inserts that prompt as if I had written it. To create a team command, I add a file such as review.md to .claude/commands/ in the repository. The file name becomes the command, so this one runs as /review. The body holds the instructions, for example what to check in a code review and how to format the output. I can add optional frontmatter such as a description and an argument hint so it is clear in the command menu. Because the folder is committed to git, every teammate who pulls the repo gets the same /review. For commands that only I need across all projects, I put the file in ~/.claude/commands/ instead.
