objective.question: You want a code-review subagent that every developer on your repository can use. Where should you save its definition file?
options: The .claude/agents/ folder in the project repository
~/.claude/settings.json under an agents key
The CLAUDE.md file at the project root
~/.claude/agents/ on each developer's machine
objective.explanation: Project subagents live in .claude/agents/ inside the repository, so they can be committed and shared. ~/.claude/agents/ is for personal, user-level subagents. CLAUDE.md and settings.json do not hold agent definitions.

objective.question: A developer has a subagent named code-reviewer in ~/.claude/agents/. The repository also has a different code-reviewer in .claude/agents/. Which one does Claude Code use inside that repository?
options: The project-level one in .claude/agents/
Neither; Claude Code reports a name conflict and loads no agent
Whichever file was modified most recently
The user-level one in ~/.claude/agents/
objective.explanation: When a project subagent and a user subagent share a name, the project-level definition takes priority. File age does not matter, and the conflict does not block loading.

objective.question: An agent definition has name, description and a system prompt, but no tools field. The main session has Edit, Bash and several MCP tools enabled. What can this subagent use?
options: All tools available to the main thread, including MCP tools
Every built-in tool, but no MCP tools
No tools until a tools field is added
Only Read, Grep and Glob, because subagents are read-only by default
objective.explanation: If tools is omitted, the subagent inherits all tools of the main thread, including MCP tools. So the subagent is not read-only, and it can edit files and run commands.

objective.question: Which tools field value gives a code-review subagent read access to the codebase and no way to change files?
options: tools: Read, Edit, Grep
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
tools: Read, Write
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
objective.explanation: Read, Grep and Glob let the agent read files, search content and find files by pattern. Edit and Write change files directly. Bash can run any shell command, which includes commands that modify files.

objective.question: Your read-only reviewer has tools: Read, Grep, Glob. A teammate wants it to run git diff on its own and suggests adding Bash. What is the best response if the reviewer must not be able to modify files?
options: Add Bash and Write so the reviewer can save its report
Keep the current tools; have the main session run git diff and pass the diff to the reviewer in the task
Remove all tools so the reviewer works only from its system prompt
Add Bash; git diff cannot change anything
objective.explanation: Bash allows any shell command, including ones that edit or delete files, so adding it breaks the read-only guarantee. The main session can produce the diff and hand it over, and the reviewer can still read related files with Read, Grep and Glob. Removing all tools would stop it from checking context.

objective.question: Which fields are required in the YAML frontmatter of a subagent file?
options: description and model
name, description, tools and model
name and description
name and tools
objective.explanation: Only name and description are required. tools and model are optional. If you leave them out, the subagent inherits all tools, and the model falls back to the default.

objective.question: You want a subagent to always use the same model the main Claude Code session is running. What should the model field contain?
options: model: main
model: same
model: inherit
model: default
objective.explanation: The model field accepts an alias such as sonnet, opus or haiku, or the value inherit, which uses the main session's model. The other values are not documented options.

objective.question: You design a planner subagent that should hand each file to a separate reviewer subagent. In testing, the planner never starts the reviewers. Why?
options: Subagents cannot start other subagents; delegation is only one level deep
The reviewers must be stored in ~/.claude/agents/ to be callable
The planner must use model: opus to delegate
The planner needs the Task tool listed in its tools field
objective.explanation: Subagents cannot spawn further subagents, so only the main session can delegate. The main session should orchestrate and call the planner and the reviewers itself. Tool lists, file location and model choice do not lift this limit.

objective.question: A reviewer subagent reads 30 files and runs many searches. What comes back into the main session's context when it finishes?
options: Nothing; you must open the subagent's log to see results
Its final result, such as the review summary
A copy of the subagent's whole context window
The full transcript of every tool call and file it read
objective.explanation: Each subagent works in its own context window and returns only a final result to the main session. That keeps the main context clean, which is a key reason to use subagents for heavy reading.

objective.question: You are working on main in ~/app and want a second Claude Code session to build a feature on a new branch at the same time, in a separate folder. Which command sets this up?
options: git worktree add ../app-feature -b feature
git clone --branch feature ../app-feature
git branch feature && claude --worktree feature
git checkout -b feature ../app-feature
objective.explanation: git worktree add ../app-feature -b feature creates a new working directory on a new branch that shares the same repository. You then cd into ../app-feature and run claude. Checkout switches branches in place, and clone makes a separate copy of the repository.

objective.question: Your feature branch from the ../app-feature worktree has been merged. What is the clean way to remove that working directory?
options: git worktree prune --all-branches
/agents remove app-feature inside Claude Code
git branch -D feature only
git worktree remove ../app-feature
objective.explanation: git worktree remove removes the working directory and its worktree record. Deleting the branch does not remove the folder. /agents manages subagents, not Git worktrees.

objective.question: You need to rename one function and update its six call sites in three closely related files. Which approach fits best?
options: One subagent per call site, run in parallel
A single Claude Code session
A planner subagent that starts editor subagents
Three parallel sessions in three worktrees, one per file
objective.explanation: The change is small and tightly coupled, so one session that keeps the whole change in view is simplest and safest. Splitting it would add merge conflicts and coordination cost. Subagents also cannot start other subagents.

objective.question: Claude Code rarely calls your code-reviewer subagent on its own, even after you make changes. Which edit is most likely to help?
options: Change model to opus
Move the file from .claude/agents/ to ~/.claude/agents/
Rewrite the description to say clearly when to use it, for example: use proactively after code changes to review the diff
Add more tools to the tools field
objective.explanation: Claude reads the description field to decide when to delegate, so a specific, action-oriented description improves automatic use. Tools, model and file location do not control when the agent is picked. You can also call it explicitly by name.

objective.question: A new team member says the reviewer subagent works for you but does not appear for them after they pull the repository. What is the most likely cause?
options: They need to use model: inherit
Subagents only load inside a Git worktree
Your reviewer file is in ~/.claude/agents/ instead of the committed .claude/agents/ folder
Subagents only work for the person who created them
objective.explanation: User-level agents in ~/.claude/agents/ exist only on your machine. To share an agent, put it in .claude/agents/ and commit that folder to Git. The model field and worktrees do not affect whether the agent is visible.

subjective.question: What is a subagent in Claude Code, and why does its separate context window matter?
subjective.answer: A subagent is a specialised assistant that the main Claude Code session can hand a task to. Each subagent has its own system prompt, its own allowed tools and its own context window. The separate context window is the key benefit. When a reviewer reads twenty files and runs many searches, all that detail stays inside the subagent. Only its final result, such as a review summary, comes back to the main session. This keeps the main conversation focused on the real task and saves context for later work. It also improves quality, because the subagent starts fresh with a narrow instruction and is not distracted by earlier chat. The trade-off is that the subagent does not see the main conversation history, so the task you give it must include everything it needs, such as the diff or the file paths.
keyPoints: Specialised assistant with its own system prompt, tools and context
Heavy reading stays inside the subagent
Only the final result returns to the main session
Fresh context gives focus but needs a complete task brief

subjective.question: Describe the agent definition file you would write for a read-only code-review subagent.
subjective.answer: I create .claude/agents/code-reviewer.md. It is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter. In the frontmatter I set name: code-reviewer. The description reads something like: reviews code changes for bugs, security issues and style; use proactively after code is modified. I set tools: Read, Grep, Glob so it can only read, search and find files. I may set model: sonnet, or inherit to match the main session. Below the frontmatter, the Markdown body is the system prompt. It tells the reviewer to focus on the supplied diff, check correctness, error handling, security, tests and naming, open related files for context, and never propose to apply changes itself. It also sets an output format, such as findings grouped as critical, warning and suggestion, each with a file and line reference. Then I commit the file so the team shares the same reviewer.
keyPoints: File in .claude/agents/ as Markdown with YAML frontmatter
name and description required; description says when to use it
tools: Read, Grep, Glob for read-only access
Body is the system prompt with review focus and output format

subjective.question: A colleague left out the tools field because they thought a reviewer would be safe by default. Explain the risk.
subjective.answer: Leaving out tools does not make a subagent restricted. It does the opposite. The subagent inherits every tool the main thread has, including Edit, Write, Bash and any MCP tools that are connected. So a reviewer meant only to comment could edit files, run shell commands, or act through an MCP server, for example by writing to a database or posting to an external service. Even if the prompt says do not edit, a prompt is guidance, not a hard limit. The tools field is the actual permission boundary. For any agent that should be read-only, I always list the tools explicitly, usually Read, Grep and Glob, and I review that line in pull requests the same way I would review access rights. Explicit allow-lists also make the agent's behaviour easier to predict and audit.
keyPoints: Omitted tools means all main-thread tools are inherited
Includes Edit, Write, Bash and MCP tools
A prompt instruction is not an enforcement mechanism
Always list tools explicitly for restricted agents

subjective.question: Explain the difference between project-level and user-level subagents and how name conflicts are resolved.
subjective.answer: Project subagents live in .claude/agents/ inside the repository. They apply only to that project, and they should be committed to Git so every developer and CI run uses the same definitions. User subagents live in ~/.claude/agents/ in my home folder. They are personal and are available in every project I open, which suits helpers that match my own workflow. If both locations have an agent with the same name, the project-level one wins. That is sensible: a team's agreed reviewer for this codebase should override someone's personal version. In practice I keep shared, project-specific agents such as code-reviewer or migration-checker in the repository, and I keep personal utilities in my home folder with distinct names so I do not shadow project agents by accident.
keyPoints: .claude/agents/ is project scope and is shared through Git
~/.claude/agents/ is user scope across all projects
Project-level wins on a name conflict
Use distinct names to avoid confusion

subjective.question: Your read-only reviewer cannot run git diff because it has no Bash. How do you still get it to review a diff?
subjective.answer: I let the main session do the Git work and keep the reviewer strictly read-only. The main session has Bash, so it runs git diff, or git diff main...HEAD for a branch, and passes the diff text to the reviewer in the task description. The reviewer then uses Read to open the full files around each change, Grep to find callers of a changed function, and Glob to locate related tests. This split is deliberate. Adding Bash would let the reviewer run any command, including ones that change or delete files, which breaks the read-only guarantee. Another option is to write the diff to a file and let the reviewer Read it. Either way, the permission boundary stays clean and the checkpoint holds: the reviewer reviews the diff but cannot edit anything.
keyPoints: Main session runs git diff and passes the output
Reviewer uses Read, Grep, Glob for surrounding context
Adding Bash breaks the read-only guarantee
Alternative: save the diff to a file the reviewer can Read

subjective.question: Walk through how you use Git worktrees to run two Claude Code sessions in parallel.
subjective.answer: A worktree is an extra working directory tied to the same repository but checked out on its own branch. From the main repo I run git worktree add ../app-feature -b feature. That creates the folder ../app-feature on a new branch called feature. I open a second terminal, cd ../app-feature and run claude. Now one session can fix a bug on main in the original folder while the other builds the feature, and they never overwrite each other's files because each has its own checkout. Both share the same Git history, so commits on one branch are visible from the other without pushing. Each worktree may need its own setup, such as installing dependencies. When the feature is merged, I run git worktree remove ../app-feature to clean up, and delete the branch if it is no longer needed.
keyPoints: git worktree add ../app-feature -b feature
cd into the folder and run claude in a separate terminal
Separate checkouts, shared repository history
Clean up with git worktree remove

subjective.question: How do you decide whether to split work across subagents or worktrees, or keep it in one session?
subjective.answer: I start from coupling and size. One session is enough when the change is small, touches closely linked files, or needs steady back-and-forth with me. Splitting it would only add coordination cost. I use a subagent when a side task needs heavy reading but only a short answer, such as code review, searching a large codebase or researching an API. The subagent keeps that noise out of the main context. I use parallel sessions in worktrees when there are truly independent pieces of work, such as a bug fix and a separate feature, that touch different areas and can be merged later. I avoid parallel work on the same files, because merge conflicts erase the time saved. I also count the cost: more sessions mean more tokens and more output for me to review.
keyPoints: Small or tightly coupled work: one session
Subagent: heavy reading with a short result
Worktrees: independent tasks in different areas
Watch merge conflicts, token cost and review load

subjective.question: Why is the description field so important, and what makes a good one?
subjective.answer: The description is what Claude reads when it decides whether to hand a task to a subagent. If it is vague, like 'helps with code', Claude may never pick the agent or may pick it for the wrong job. A good description states what the agent does and when to use it, in concrete terms. For example: 'Expert code reviewer. Reviews diffs for bugs, security issues and readability. Use proactively after code changes.' Words like 'use proactively' encourage automatic delegation. I keep each agent focused on one job so descriptions do not overlap; if two agents claim the same work, the choice becomes unpredictable. When I need certainty, I do not rely on automatic selection and instead ask for the agent by name, for example 'use the code-reviewer subagent on this diff'.
keyPoints: Claude uses description to choose when to delegate
State what it does and when to use it
Phrases like use proactively encourage automatic use
Avoid overlapping agents; invoke by name when needed

subjective.question: Subagents cannot start other subagents. How does that shape your design?
subjective.answer: Delegation is one level deep. Only the main session can call subagents, so I treat the main session as the orchestrator. If I want to review a large change, I do not build a reviewer that spawns per-file reviewers. Instead, the main session splits the work and calls the reviewer several times, or calls different specialist agents such as a security reviewer and a test checker, then combines their results. Each subagent must be self-contained: it gets a complete brief and returns one final result. This keeps the system simple and easier to debug, because there is no deep tree of agents talking to each other. It also means I should not give a subagent a prompt that tells it to delegate, because it simply cannot.
keyPoints: Delegation is one level deep
Main session acts as orchestrator
Subagents need complete, self-contained briefs
Combine multiple subagent results in the main session

subjective.question: How do you choose the model field for a subagent?
subjective.answer: The model field is optional and accepts an alias, sonnet, opus or haiku, or inherit to use the main session's model. I choose based on how hard the task is and how often it runs. A quick read-only explorer that searches files and summarises structure can use haiku, which is faster and cheaper. A code reviewer that must reason about correctness and security deserves sonnet, or opus for complex or high-risk code. I use inherit when I want the subagent to follow whatever model the developer has chosen for the session, which keeps behaviour consistent. Cost matters with subagents because each one consumes its own tokens, and parallel use multiplies that. I test the agent on real diffs before settling the model, because a cheaper model that misses bugs is not a saving.
keyPoints: Accepts sonnet, opus, haiku or inherit
Match model to task difficulty and frequency
inherit follows the main session's model
Each subagent uses its own tokens; test before choosing

subjective.question: How would you prove the checkpoint: that your reviewer reviews a diff but cannot edit files?
subjective.answer: First I check the definition. The frontmatter must list tools: Read, Grep, Glob and nothing else, so no Edit, Write, Bash or MCP tools. I also confirm in /agents that the reviewer shows only those tools. Next, I make a small change with a deliberate bug, run git diff in the main session and ask the code-reviewer subagent to review it. It should report the bug with a file and line reference. Then I test the boundary. I ask the reviewer to fix the bug itself. It should not have any tool that can change a file. Finally, I run git status and git diff again to confirm no extra changes appeared. Only the main session should apply fixes, after I read the review.
keyPoints: Frontmatter lists only Read, Grep, Glob
Confirm the tool list in /agents
Seed a known bug and check it is reported
Ask it to fix; verify with git status that nothing changed

subjective.question: What does the /agents command do, and when would you use it instead of writing the file by hand?
subjective.answer: /agents opens an interactive manager inside Claude Code. From there I can see all available subagents, built-in, user and project, and create, edit or delete them. When creating one, it asks whether it should be a project or user agent and lets me pick tools from a list, which shows exactly what the agent can use, including MCP tools. It can also help draft the description and system prompt. I use /agents when I am starting out, when I want a quick check of which tools an agent actually has, or when MCP servers add tools I may not remember. I write the file by hand when I already know the definition, want precise wording, or am copying a team standard. Either way, the result is the same Markdown file with YAML frontmatter.
keyPoints: Interactive manager for listing, creating, editing, deleting agents
Choose project or user scope
Tool picker shows exact access, including MCP tools
Produces the same Markdown plus frontmatter file

subjective.question: Claude Code has built-in subagents. How do they relate to custom agents you write?
subjective.answer: Claude Code ships with a general-purpose subagent that can handle multi-step tasks with broad tool access. Recent versions also include built-in Explore and Plan agents, which are aimed at read-only work: exploring a codebase, finding where things live and researching before changes are made. These cover many common needs without any setup, so I do not write a custom agent just to search the code. I write custom agents when I need something the built-ins do not give me: a team-specific review checklist, a fixed output format, a deliberately narrow tool set, or a chosen model. A custom code-reviewer with Read, Grep and Glob and our own standards is a good example. Custom agents live in .claude/agents/, can be committed, and give the whole team repeatable behaviour.
keyPoints: Built-in general-purpose agent for multi-step tasks
Explore and Plan for read-only exploration and research
Use built-ins for generic needs
Custom agents add team standards, strict tools and formats

subjective.question: What problems can appear when running several Claude Code sessions in parallel worktrees, and how do you manage them?
subjective.answer: The main risk is merge conflicts. If two sessions change the same files, the time saved is lost when merging, so I only run work in parallel when the areas are clearly separate. Second, worktrees share one repository but not the working files, so each folder may need its own dependency install, build output and environment files. Third, shared local resources can clash, for example two dev servers on the same port or two test runs using the same local database. I give each worktree its own port or test database. Fourth, review load grows, because I must read every session's output carefully. Finally, stale worktrees pile up, so I run git worktree list to check and git worktree remove when a branch is merged. Rebasing branches on main regularly keeps conflicts small.
keyPoints: Split only independent areas to avoid merge conflicts
Each worktree needs its own setup and environment
Avoid clashes on ports and local databases
Review each session; clean up with git worktree list and remove

steps.overview: This step takes Claude Code out of the interactive terminal and into automation. You will run Claude non-interactively with `claude -p`, wire it into GitHub Actions so it reviews pull requests and fixes issues, and see how the Claude Agent SDK exposes the same agent loop for your own programs. Cost and context control is the thread through all three, because unattended runs can loop, overspend or leak permissions if you do not bound them.
objectives: Run Claude Code headlessly with `claude -p`, choosing output format, turn limits, model and allowed tools for a script.
Configure `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` with secrets, permissions and a prompt so it posts a review on every pull request.
Explain when to use headless CLI, the GitHub Action or the Claude Agent SDK for an automation task.
Build a minimal agent with the Claude Agent SDK `query()` function and restrict its tools.
Control cost and context in automated runs using turn limits, model choice, narrow tool lists and JSON cost output.

concepts.explanation: `claude -p "prompt"` (long form `--print`) runs one agentic task without the interactive UI, prints the result and exits. You can pipe input into it, for example `git diff | claude -p "review this"`. It is the base for scripts, cron jobs, pre-commit checks and CI. Permission prompts cannot be answered here, so you must pre-approve tools or the run will be blocked.

`--output-format text` is the default and prints only the final answer. `json` returns one object with fields such as `result`, `session_id`, `num_turns`, `duration_ms` and `total_cost_usd`, which is ideal for scripts. `stream-json` emits one JSON message per line as the agent works, so you can show live progress or parse tool calls.

`--allowedTools` pre-approves specific tools, with patterns like `Bash(npm test:*)` or `Bash(gh pr comment:*)`. `--disallowedTools` blocks tools. `--permission-mode` sets modes such as `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan` or `bypassPermissions`. In CI, grant the narrowest list that does the job instead of skipping all permissions.

Every headless run has a `session_id`. `--continue` resumes the most recent conversation and `--resume <session_id>` resumes a specific one, so a script can run multi-step work across calls. `--max-turns` caps how many agent loop iterations a run may take, which bounds time and cost.

`anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` runs Claude Code inside a GitHub Actions runner. In interactive mode it reacts to a trigger phrase (default `@claude`) in PR or issue comments. In automation mode you give it a `prompt` input, so it runs on events such as `pull_request` with no mention needed. Extra CLI flags go in the `claude_args` input.

Inside Claude Code, the `/install-github-app` command installs the Claude GitHub App on your repo and adds the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret. You need repo admin rights. Manual setup means installing the app, adding the secret yourself and committing a workflow file under `.github/workflows/`. Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex AI are also supported through action inputs and OIDC.

The Claude Agent SDK (formerly the Claude Code SDK) gives you the same agent loop, tools and context management that power Claude Code, as a library. Python package `claude-agent-sdk` (import `claude_agent_sdk`) and TypeScript package `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`. `query()` streams messages for a one-off task, and `ClaudeSDKClient` keeps a multi-turn session. Options such as `allowed_tools`, `system_prompt`, `max_turns`, `cwd` and `mcp_servers` are set via `ClaudeAgentOptions`.

concepts.term: SDK defaults vs Claude Code defaults
concepts.explanation: By default the Agent SDK does not load filesystem settings such as CLAUDE.md or `.claude/settings.json`; you opt in with `setting_sources`. Its default system prompt is minimal, and you can use the `claude_code` preset to get Claude Code behaviour. This isolation is deliberate, so your production agent behaves the same on every machine.

Each turn re-sends context, so long sessions and big files cost more. Interactively use `/cost`, `/context`, `/compact` and `/clear`. In automation, set `--max-turns`, pick a fitting `--model`, limit tools, keep prompts focused on the diff, and log `total_cost_usd` from JSON output. Prompt caching is applied automatically and lowers the cost of repeated context.

keyFacts: `-p` = `--print`: non-interactive, one task, then exit; stdin can be piped in as context.
`--output-format` values: `text` (default), `json`, `stream-json`; JSON includes `total_cost_usd` and `session_id`.
`--max-turns N` limits agent loop iterations; always set it in CI to prevent runaway runs.
Action reference: `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`; API key input `anthropic_api_key`, task input `prompt`, CLI flags via `claude_args`.
Default interactive trigger phrase is `@claude`; supplying `prompt` switches the action to automation mode with no mention needed.
Typical workflow permissions: `contents: read`, `pull-requests: write`, `issues: write`, plus `id-token: write` for the app or OIDC (Bedrock/Vertex).
Store the key as the repository secret `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and reference it as `${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}`; never hard-code it.
Secrets are not passed to `pull_request` workflows triggered from forks, so the review job fails on fork PRs unless you redesign the trigger carefully.
Agent SDK packages: `claude-agent-sdk` (Python) and `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` (TypeScript); renamed from Claude Code SDK.
Decision rule: shell script or one-off pipeline → `claude -p`; repo events on GitHub → the Action; your own product or custom agent → Agent SDK.

example.caption: .github/workflows/claude-review.yml: review every non-draft PR and post one comment
example.code:
name: Claude PR Review
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]
jobs:
  review:
    if: github.event.pull_request.draft == false
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
      issues: write
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 1
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          prompt: |
            REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
            PR NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
            Review this PR for bugs, security issues and missing tests.
            Be concise. Post ONE summary comment using gh pr comment.
          claude_args: |
            --max-turns 8
            --allowedTools "Bash(gh pr diff:*),Bash(gh pr view:*),Bash(gh pr comment:*),Read,Grep,Glob"

pitfalls: Running `claude -p` in CI without `--allowedTools`: the agent hits a permission prompt nobody can answer, and the run stops without doing the work.
Using `--dangerously-skip-permissions` or `bypassPermissions` on a shared runner. Prefer a narrow allow-list; full bypass only belongs in an isolated sandbox or container.
Forgetting `pull-requests: write` (or the `issues: write` the comment API needs). The review runs but the comment never appears, which is the most common checkpoint failure.
No `--max-turns` and no draft filter: every push to a large PR triggers a long, costly review. Skip drafts, cap turns and scope the prompt to the diff.
Assuming the Agent SDK reads your CLAUDE.md and settings automatically. It does not unless you set `setting_sources`.
Calling it the 'Claude Code SDK' with old package names in answers. The current name is Claude Agent SDK.

objective.question: A developer runs `claude -p "Summarise the TODOs in src/"` from a shell script. What does the `-p` flag do?
options: Runs Claude Code non-interactively for one task, prints the result and exits
Pins the session so it can be resumed later with the same ID
Enables plan mode so Claude only proposes changes
Opens the interactive REPL with the prompt pre-filled
objective.explanation: `-p` is short for `--print`. It runs a single non-interactive task, prints the output and exits. It does not open the REPL. Plan mode is set with `--permission-mode plan`, not `-p`.

objective.question: Your nightly script calls `claude -p` and must log how much each run cost, so it can alert if spend spikes. Which flag gives you a machine-readable cost field?
options: `--verbose`
`--max-turns 1`
`--output-format json`
`--output-format text`
objective.explanation: JSON output returns a result object with fields such as `total_cost_usd` and `session_id`, which a script can parse. Plain text gives only the answer. `--verbose` adds logging detail and `--max-turns` limits loop iterations, but neither is a cost field.

objective.question: A CI job that uses `claude -p` to fix lint errors ran for 40 minutes and burned a lot of tokens, because the agent kept retrying. What is the most direct guardrail to add?
options: `--continue`
A longer GitHub Actions `timeout-minutes` value
`--output-format stream-json`
`--max-turns` with a sensible limit
objective.explanation: `--max-turns N` caps the number of agent loop iterations, so a runaway run stops early. Stream-json only changes the output shape. `--continue` resumes a conversation. A longer job timeout makes the problem worse.

objective.question: What happens when you run `git diff main | claude -p "Review this diff for security issues"`?
options: The diff becomes the prompt and the quoted text is discarded
The piped diff is passed in as context along with the prompt, and Claude prints its review
The command fails because `-p` cannot accept piped input
Claude ignores stdin and reads the whole repository instead
objective.explanation: In print mode, stdin can be piped in as context. Claude combines the piped content with your prompt. This is a common pattern for reviewing diffs, logs or test output in scripts.

objective.question: You use `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` and want Claude to review every pull request automatically, with no one typing `@claude`. What makes the action behave this way?
options: Supplying the `prompt` input, which switches the action to automation mode
Adding `--dangerously-skip-permissions` in `claude_args`
Granting `id-token: write` to the job
Setting `trigger_phrase` to an empty string
objective.explanation: When you supply `prompt`, the action runs in automation mode and executes the task on the workflow trigger, with no mention needed. Without it, the action waits for the default trigger phrase `@claude`. Permissions flags and token scopes do not change the mode.

objective.question: In a v1 workflow, you want to limit the review to 5 turns and choose a specific model. Where do these CLI options go?
options: In separate `max_turns` and `model` inputs, as in the beta
In environment variables `CLAUDE_MAX_TURNS` and `CLAUDE_MODEL`
In the `prompt` text itself
In the `claude_args` input

objective.question: Your PR review workflow runs successfully, but the step that posts the review comment fails with a 403 error. The job has only `contents: read`. What is the minimum change?
options: Add `pull-requests: write`
Add `id-token: write`

objective.question: Your company does not allow direct Anthropic API keys. It runs Claude through Amazon Bedrock and authenticates from GitHub Actions using OIDC. Which workflow permission is required for this?

`security-events: write`

objective.question: The PR review workflow uses `on: pull_request` and reads `${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}`. It works for team branches, but fails on every pull request from an outside contributor's fork. What is the cause?
options: Fork PRs must use the `@claude` trigger phrase
The `prompt` input is ignored on forks
GitHub does not pass repository secrets to `pull_request` workflows triggered from forks, so the API key is empty

objective.question: Your product team wants a customer-facing support agent inside your own web app. It should reuse Claude Code's agent loop and tools but have its own UI and custom tools. Which option fits best?
options: Claude Code GitHub Actions triggered by issues
The Claude Agent SDK
An interactive Claude Code session left running on a server
A bash script that calls `claude -p` for each customer message
objective.explanation: The decision rule is: your own product or custom agent goes to the Agent SDK. `claude -p` suits shell scripts and one-off pipelines. The Action suits GitHub repo events. An interactive session is not a production integration.

objective.question: You build an agent with the Agent SDK in a repository that has a detailed `CLAUDE.md`. The agent ignores the project conventions in that file. What is the most likely reason?
options: The SDK only reads `CLAUDE.md` when it is placed in the home directory
`CLAUDE.md` is only supported in the TypeScript SDK
The SDK reads `CLAUDE.md` only when `--max-turns` is set
By default the SDK does not load filesystem settings such as `CLAUDE.md`; you must opt in, for example through setting sources
objective.explanation: The Agent SDK has different defaults from the Claude Code CLI. It does not load project settings or `CLAUDE.md` unless you configure setting sources, and it does not use the Claude Code system prompt unless you request the preset. This gives SDK apps predictable, isolated behaviour.

objective.question: A script runs `claude -p` with JSON output, saves the `session_id`, and later needs to ask a follow-up in that exact conversation, even though other sessions have run since. Which approach is correct?
options: `claude -p --resume <session_id> "follow-up"`
Pipe the previous JSON output into a new `claude -p` call
Run `claude -p` with the same prompt and rely on caching
`claude -p --continue "follow-up"`
objective.explanation: `--resume` with a session ID resumes that specific conversation. `--continue` picks the most recent conversation in the directory, which may be the wrong one if other runs happened. Piping old output only gives text context, not the real session.

objective.question: You want a headless CI review job that can read and search code but must never edit files or run arbitrary shell commands. What is the best configuration?
options: Leave permissions at default; CI has no terminal, so tools cannot run
Use `--permission-mode acceptEdits`
Allow only read-only tools such as `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` with `--allowedTools`, and disallow write and shell tools
Use `--dangerously-skip-permissions` so the job never blocks
objective.explanation: In automation there is no human to approve prompts, so you explicitly allow only the tools the task needs. Skipping permissions gives the agent full power on the runner. `acceptEdits` auto-approves file edits, which is the opposite of what you want.

objective.question: Automated PR reviews on a large monorepo cost far more than expected. Which change most directly reduces cost per review without losing review value?
options: Remove `--max-turns` so the agent finishes in one long pass
Trigger the review on every push to every branch as well as on PRs
Scope the prompt to the changed files, set a turn limit, and pick a model that fits the task
Switch output to `stream-json`
objective.explanation: Cost follows tokens and turns. Focusing on the diff keeps the context small, a turn cap prevents long loops, and choosing a fitting model controls the price per token. Output format does not change token usage, and more triggers mean more runs.

subjective.question: What is headless mode in Claude Code, and when would you use it instead of an interactive session?
subjective.answer: Headless mode is `claude -p`, which is short for `--print`. You give one task, Claude runs the agent loop without any interactive prompts, prints the result and exits. Because it is non-interactive, it fits places where no human is watching: shell scripts, cron jobs, git hooks, Makefile targets and CI pipelines. You can also pipe data in through stdin, for example `cat error.log | claude -p "explain the root cause"`, and the piped content becomes context. I use interactive mode for exploring, pairing and multi-step work where I want to steer. I use headless mode when the task is repeatable and well-defined, such as generating a changelog from a diff, classifying test failures or running a lint fix. In headless runs I always set `--max-turns`, restrict tools, and use JSON output when another program will consume the result.
keyPoints: `-p` equals `--print`: one task, non-interactive, then exit
stdin can be piped in as context
Fits scripts, hooks, cron and CI
Interactive mode is for exploration and steering
Add guardrails: turn limit, tool limits, structured output

subjective.question: Compare the three `--output-format` values for `claude -p` and say when you would pick each.
subjective.answer: `text` is the default. It prints only the final answer as plain text, which is fine when a human reads it or when you redirect it to a file such as release notes. `json` returns a single JSON object at the end of the run. It holds the result plus metadata such as `total_cost_usd`, `session_id` and run details, so it is the right choice when a script must parse the output, record spend or save the session ID to resume later. `stream-json` emits a stream of JSON messages as the run progresses. It suits long tasks where you want live progress, logs of each tool call, or a UI that shows events in real time. My rule: humans read text, scripts parse json, and live dashboards or long-running pipelines consume stream-json.
keyPoints: `text` is the default, plain final answer
`json` gives one object with `total_cost_usd` and `session_id`
`stream-json` streams messages during the run
Pick based on who consumes the output

subjective.question: Why should you always set `--max-turns` in CI, and how would you choose the value?
subjective.answer: An agent works in a loop: think, call a tool, read the result, repeat. In CI nobody is watching. If the agent gets stuck, for example retrying a failing test or searching for a file that does not exist, it can keep looping, which wastes runner minutes and tokens and may make unwanted changes. `--max-turns N` puts a hard cap on loop iterations, so the run ends predictably. To choose the value, I first run the task manually and note how many turns a normal success takes. Then I set the limit a little above that. A focused PR review might need only a handful of turns, while a bug fix that edits files and runs tests needs more. I also treat hitting the limit as a signal: I log it and check whether the prompt or the task scope needs tightening.
keyPoints: Agent loop can run away with no human present
Cap protects cost, time and repo safety
Base the value on observed normal runs plus headroom
Hitting the cap is a signal to fix the prompt or scope

subjective.question: How do you handle tool permissions safely when Claude Code runs in automation?
subjective.answer: Interactively, Claude asks before risky actions. In automation there is no one to answer, so I decide the permissions up front and follow least privilege. I use `--allowedTools` to list exactly what the task needs. A reviewer gets read-only tools like `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`. A fixer may also get `Edit` and narrowly scoped `Bash` patterns, such as only the test command. I use `--disallowedTools` to block dangerous ones explicitly. I avoid `--dangerously-skip-permissions` except inside a disposable, isolated container with no secrets and no network access it does not need. I also limit the GitHub token scopes in the workflow, so even if the agent misbehaves, it cannot push to protected branches. Finally, permissions should be committed in config or in the workflow file, so they are reviewed like code.
keyPoints: No human to approve, so decide permissions in advance
`--allowedTools` and `--disallowedTools` for least privilege
Read-only tools for reviews; scoped Bash for fixes
Avoid skipping permissions outside isolated sandboxes
Limit GitHub token scopes too

subjective.question: Explain session control in headless mode. What is the difference between `--continue` and `--resume`, and which is safer in scripts?
subjective.answer: Every Claude Code run creates a session with an ID. Session control lets a later run carry on from an earlier conversation, keeping its context, instead of starting cold. `--continue`, or `-c`, picks up the most recent conversation in the current directory. That is convenient at the terminal but risky in scripts, because if another run happened in between, you continue the wrong conversation. `--resume` with a session ID, or `-r`, resumes one specific conversation. In scripts I run the first step with `--output-format json`, read `session_id` from the result, store it, and pass it to `--resume` for follow-up steps. That is deterministic and safe when jobs run in parallel. I also remember that resumed sessions carry the old context, so long chains grow in tokens and cost; sometimes a fresh run with a short summary is cheaper.
keyPoints: Each run has a session ID
`--continue` resumes the most recent conversation
`--resume <id>` targets a specific session
Capture `session_id` from JSON output in scripts
Resumed context adds token cost

subjective.question: Walk me through a GitHub Actions workflow that reviews every pull request with Claude.
subjective.answer: I create `.github/workflows/claude-review.yml`. The trigger is `on: pull_request` with types `opened` and `synchronize`, so it runs on new PRs and new pushes. The job runs on `ubuntu-latest` with permissions `contents: read` and `pull-requests: write`, and `id-token: write` if I use the GitHub app token flow or OIDC. Steps: first `actions/checkout`, then `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`. I pass `anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}`, with the key stored as a repository secret, never hard-coded. I give a `prompt` such as: review this PR for bugs, security and readability, focus on changed files, and post concise comments. Supplying `prompt` puts the action in automation mode, so no `@claude` mention is needed. In `claude_args` I set `--max-turns` and, if needed, `--model` and allowed tools. To check it, I open a test PR and confirm the review comment appears.
keyPoints: Trigger on `pull_request` opened and synchronize
Permissions: contents read, pull-requests write, id-token write if needed
`anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` with `anthropic_api_key` from secrets
`prompt` gives automation mode; `claude_args` for flags
Verify with a test PR

subjective.question: The Claude Code Action has an interactive mode and an automation mode. Explain both and give a use case for each.
subjective.answer: In interactive mode, the action listens for a trigger phrase, `@claude` by default, in PR comments, review comments or issues. When someone writes, for example, "@claude fix the null check in this function", the action starts, reads the context and responds or pushes a change. It suits on-demand help: answering questions on a PR, implementing a small fix from an issue, or explaining code during review. In automation mode, you supply the `prompt` input. The action then runs that task every time the workflow trigger fires, with no mention needed. It suits standard, repeatable jobs such as reviewing every pull request, triaging new issues with labels, or a scheduled dependency check. Many teams use both: automation for a baseline review on every PR, and interactive mode so reviewers can ask follow-ups. The trigger phrase can be changed with an input if `@claude` clashes with something.
keyPoints: Interactive: triggered by `@claude` mention
Automation: `prompt` input, runs on every trigger
Interactive for on-demand fixes and questions
Automation for consistent reviews and triage
Both can coexist in one repo

subjective.question: What does `/install-github-app` do, what do you need before running it, and when would you set things up manually instead?
subjective.answer: `/install-github-app` is a command you run inside Claude Code in your repository's terminal. It guides you through installing the Claude GitHub app on the repo, adding the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret, and creating a starter workflow file, usually through a pull request you can review. Before running it, you need admin rights on the repository, because installing apps and adding secrets need them, and you need the GitHub CLI authenticated. It works for direct Anthropic API users. I would set things up manually when the company uses Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex AI with OIDC, when security policy requires its own GitHub app or restricted secrets, when org admins must approve app installs, or when I need a custom workflow with specific triggers, permissions and tool limits. Manual setup means installing the app, adding secrets and writing the YAML yourself.
keyPoints: Run inside Claude Code in the repo
Installs the app, adds the secret, creates a workflow
Needs repo admin rights and an authenticated GitHub CLI
Manual setup for Bedrock/Vertex, strict policies or custom workflows

subjective.question: Your PR review workflow fails on pull requests from forks. Explain why, and discuss safe ways to handle it.
subjective.answer: GitHub does not pass repository secrets to `pull_request` workflows triggered from forks. That protects the repo, because a fork author could otherwise change the workflow or code to print the secret. So `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is empty and the review step fails. One option is `pull_request_target`, which runs in the context of the base repo and has secrets. But it is dangerous: if the job checks out and executes the fork's code, an attacker can steal secrets or abuse a write token. If I use it, I do not run untrusted code, I keep permissions minimal, and I gate runs behind a label that a maintainer adds after a quick look, or a required environment approval. A simpler choice for open source is to skip the automated review on forks and let maintainers trigger it after a manual check. Either way, I never weaken secret handling just to make the job green.
keyPoints: Secrets are not passed to fork `pull_request` runs
`pull_request_target` has secrets but is risky with untrusted code
Mitigate with labels, environment approvals, minimal permissions
Option to skip forks or trigger manually
Never expose or hard-code the key

subjective.question: What is the Claude Agent SDK, and how does it relate to Claude Code?
subjective.answer: The Claude Agent SDK is a library for building your own agents on the same agent loop that powers Claude Code. It was previously called the Claude Code SDK and was renamed because people use it for far more than coding agents, such as support, research or operations agents. It comes as `claude-agent-sdk` for Python and `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` for TypeScript. With it, your code sends a prompt and receives a stream of messages while the agent reasons, calls tools and returns results. You get the built-in tools like file reading, editing and shell, plus context management, permission control, MCP server support, subagents and hooks. You can add custom tools for your own systems. So Claude Code is a ready-made product for developers, and the Agent SDK is the engine you embed in your own application with your own UI and rules.
keyPoints: Same agent loop as Claude Code
Renamed from Claude Code SDK
Packages: `claude-agent-sdk` and `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`
Built-in tools, MCP, permissions, hooks, custom tools
Use it to embed agents in your own product

subjective.question: How do the Agent SDK's defaults differ from Claude Code CLI defaults, and why does it matter?
subjective.answer: The Claude Code CLI is set up for a developer in a repo. It uses the Claude Code system prompt and loads settings from disk, including user and project settings and `CLAUDE.md`. The Agent SDK is more isolated by default. It does not apply the full Claude Code system prompt unless you ask for the `claude_code` preset, and it does not load filesystem settings or `CLAUDE.md` unless you configure setting sources. Anthropic made this choice so SDK apps behave predictably and are not changed by whatever files sit on a machine. It matters because a team may build an agent, test it on a laptop, and expect it to follow `CLAUDE.md` rules, but it will not. Or a production agent may need a fully custom system prompt. So I set the system prompt, setting sources, allowed tools and permission mode explicitly in the SDK options, and test with those exact options.
keyPoints: CLI loads Claude Code system prompt and settings by default
SDK does not load the preset system prompt unless requested
SDK does not load filesystem settings or `CLAUDE.md` unless configured
Isolation gives predictable production behaviour
Set options explicitly and test with them

subjective.question: A team asks for three things: a nightly cron that summarises failed tests, an automatic review on every PR, and an AI assistant inside their internal admin portal. Which tool would you use for each, and why?
subjective.answer: I apply the decision rule. For the nightly cron, I use `claude -p`. It is a shell-level pipeline: pipe the test report into `claude -p` with a clear prompt, set `--max-turns`, use JSON output if another script consumes it, and send the summary to Slack or email. For the PR review, I use Claude Code GitHub Actions, `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`, because the trigger is a repo event. It handles checkout context, PR comments and GitHub permissions, and the `prompt` input runs it automatically on every pull request. For the admin portal assistant, I use the Claude Agent SDK. It is part of their own product, needs a custom UI, custom tools connected to internal APIs, its own permission rules and session handling. Using `claude -p` there would be fragile, and the Action only runs inside GitHub. Picking the right layer keeps each solution simple and maintainable.
keyPoints: Shell scripts and one-off pipelines: `claude -p`
GitHub repo events: the Action
Own product or custom agent: Agent SDK
Justify by trigger, integration and control needs

subjective.question: How do you stay aware of cost and context when running Claude Code in automation?
subjective.answer: Cost depends on tokens in and out, the number of turns and the model. In automation the runs repeat, so small waste multiplies. First, I measure: JSON output gives `total_cost_usd` per run, which I log and watch over time. Second, I keep context small. I pass only what matters, such as the diff instead of the whole repo, and keep the prompt focused. A lean `CLAUDE.md` helps, because it is loaded into context. Third, I cap the loop with `--max-turns` and restrict tools so the agent does not wander. Fourth, I pick a model that fits the job: a lighter model may be enough for triage, while complex reviews may justify a stronger one. Fifth, I control triggers, for example running reviews on PR open and new pushes, not every branch push. Interactively, `/cost` shows session spend and `/compact` or `/clear` manage growing context.
keyPoints: Log `total_cost_usd` from JSON output
Send only relevant context; keep `CLAUDE.md` lean
Cap turns and restrict tools
Match the model to the task
Limit triggers; use `/cost`, `/compact`, `/clear` interactively

subjective.question: You added the PR review workflow, but after opening a test PR no review comment appears. How do you troubleshoot it?
subjective.answer: I start in the Actions tab. If the workflow did not run at all, I check the trigger: is the file in `.github/workflows` on the default branch, and does `on: pull_request` include `opened` and `synchronize`? If it ran and failed, I read the logs. An authentication error usually means the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret is missing, misnamed, or the PR came from a fork, where secrets are not passed. A 403 when posting means missing `pull-requests: write`, or an app token problem that needs `id-token: write` or the GitHub app installed. If the job succeeded but nothing was posted, I check that I supplied `prompt`, because without it the action waits for `@claude`, and that the prompt asks Claude to post comments. I also check whether it hit `--max-turns` before finishing, and whether allowed tools block commenting. I fix one thing at a time and push again.
keyPoints: Check whether the workflow triggered at all
Auth errors: secret name, fork PRs
403: `pull-requests: write`, app or `id-token` setup
No comment: missing `prompt`, turn limit, tool restrictions
Fix one thing at a time and retest

The certificates show you finished the material, and the repository is what interviewers actually check.

Download each certificate of completion and add it to LinkedIn under Licenses & certifications with Anthropic as the issuer.

concepts.explanation: This is Anthropic's free learning portal for courses on Claude, Claude Code, MCP and the API. Courses are self-paced video and text lessons with quizzes. When you finish all required lessons and quizzes, you get a certificate of completion. It is not a proctored professional exam.

This course covers how a coding assistant uses tools, and how to set up Claude Code. It teaches you to give context with CLAUDE.md, /init and @-mentions, and to control context with Escape, /clear and /compact. It also covers plan mode and thinking, custom slash commands, MCP servers, GitHub integration, hooks and the Claude Code SDK. Expect quiz questions on which feature solves which problem.

This course teaches the MCP client–server architecture and the three server primitives: tools (called by the model), resources (data the application exposes) and prompts (templates the user picks). You build a server with the Python SDK and test it with the MCP Inspector. Know who controls each primitive, because that is a common quiz theme.

This optional course covers the Messages API, multi-turn conversations, system prompts, temperature and streaming. It also teaches prompt evaluation, prompt engineering, tool use, RAG, extended thinking, image and PDF input, citations and prompt caching. It closes with MCP and with agent and workflow patterns. It gives you the API view behind what Claude Code does for you.

This is a certificate issued when you finish a course, usually with a shareable link or a downloadable file. It proves you finished the course, not that you passed a supervised exam. Describe it honestly on your CV and LinkedIn as a course completion.

This is a public Git repository that proves your skills. It should contain a CLAUDE.md, a .claude/commands folder, hooks in .claude/settings.json, an MCP configuration (.mcp.json) and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs Claude. A README should link each artifact to the course module that taught it.

Hooks are shell commands that Claude Code runs automatically at lifecycle events. The most common are PreToolUse, which can block a tool call, and PostToolUse, which runs after a tool call, for example to format or type-check code. You configure them in settings files with a matcher on tool names. Exit code 2 from a PreToolUse hook blocks the action and sends stderr back to Claude.

Claude Code can run non-interactively with `claude -p` (headless mode). It can also run in GitHub through the official Claude Code GitHub Action, which you can set up with the /install-github-app command. The API key is stored as a repository secret, never committed to the repository.

keyFacts: All three Anthropic Academy courses on this path are free and award a certificate of completion, not a proctored credential.

Custom slash commands are Markdown files in .claude/commands/. The file name becomes the command name, and $ARGUMENTS passes input to the command.

Use the MCP Inspector to test a server before you connect it to Claude Code. Add servers with `claude mcp add` or a project-level .mcp.json.

Putting personal preferences in the shared .claude/settings.json. Use .claude/settings.local.json or user settings for them.
